data.title: Canadian investors warn Burnham over Thames Water
data.description:
Mark Carney has intervened over the potential nationalisation of Thames Water after the Canadian government warned that it could damage foreign investment in Britain.

Canadian officials are growing increasingly concerned that any decision by Andy Burnham to place Thames Water under state control could result in heavy losses for overseas investors.

Ottawa is thought to have cautioned that any expropriation of privately owned assets without accompanying compensation could jeopardise further investment in the UK economy. Canada’s so-called Maple Eight pension funds, and its banks have poured tens of billions into airports, ports, the energy sectors, key utilities and property.

The dramatic intervention underscores mounting anxiety about the Prime Minister’s hostility towards the private sector. Mr Burnham has promised to “end neo-liberalism” and undo Margaret Thatcher’s legacy of privatisation and deregulation.

Yet private property rights are a fundamental pillar of the UK’s legal and economic system, and one of the key protections that make Britain a top destination for overseas capital.

Ottawa was lobbying primarily on behalf of the Royal Bank of Canada (RBC), the country’s national bank champion. It is not known whether the Canadian officials were acting on the instructions of RBC senior figures or independently.

The discussions are understood to have occurred in recent weeks. Mr Carney met the Prime Minister on a visit to Liverpool last month where the pair watched Everton football club, who they both support.

RBC is a senior creditor to Thames Water, and is among a consortium of more than 100 financial institutions that has proposed a £16bn rescue package in which around a third of the supplier’s borrowings would be written off in return for ownership.

However, many of the creditors fear being wiped out if ministers follow through with a threat to seize control of the company instead. Industry sources insist RBC’s concerns are shared by many of the other lenders to Thames.

Both Ofwat and ministers have refused to give the proposal their blessing. Instead, Burnham has made repeated yet vague threats to exert greater “public control” over the failing water industry. It is these remarks that prompted Canadian officials to intervene.

A creditor told The Telegraph: “We are still trying to understand what ‘public control’ is, and what the Government wants to do with Thames. None of us know the answer.”

Another said: “They are not looking for abnormal treatment. They just want fair value, whether that’s through nationalisation or a financial restructuring, and for their security to be respected.”

The uncertainty threatens to derail discussions about another round of rescue funding for Thames Water. Having already lent the company £3bn to keep it afloat for the last 18 months, creditors have been asked to provide another £2.4bn of liquidity.

Earlier this month, Dave Mackay, RBC’s chief executive, warned the UK Government about the risks of creating a more hostile environment for foreign and private capital.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, he said: “When the UK flirts with nationalising … Thames Water, with putting on a bank tax, with putting a capital tax on the wealthy or housing, it sends a signal you want to harvest your economy, not grow it.”

RBC has also privately expressed frustration at the failure to distinguish between institutional investors who are longstanding lenders to Thames Water and some of the more opportunistic funds seeking to profit directly from Thames’s financial predicament.

In September, a cross-party committee of MPs urged ministers to reject the creditors’ recapitalisation plan.

The environment, food and rural affairs committee criticised the “opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds and others” who are seeking to take control of Thames Water and said the Government should consider placing the utility into special administration, a form of temporary nationalisation.

However, a source close to the creditors said more than half of its lenders – including RBC – would not consider themselves to be hedge funds.

“Many of those that are being unfairly stigmatised are long-term holders of UK assets,” the person said.

A spokesman for Carney’s office said: “Prime Minister Carney has not raised the issue mentioned, neither with Prime Minister Burnham or members of his team.

“Additionally, Canada has not raised this issue at the officials level either. The Prime Minister’s Office was not contacted prior to the publishing of this story.”

RBC and a spokesman for the creditors declined to comment. Canada’s Department for Foreign Affairs was approached for comment.

data.title: Chinese imports ‘threaten to wipe out UK industries in five years’
data.description:
Cut-price Chinese manufacturers could wipe out whole chunks of British industry within five years, a think tank has warned.

Chatham House said European and UK industries ranging from electric vehicles and machine tools, to wind turbines and pharmaceuticals were “on a trajectory to lose” to China’s fast-growing and technologically dominant companies.

“There is a real possibility that over the next five years, Europe will lose much of its industrial base to Chinese competition,” said James Kynge, a Chatham House fellow and author of a new report on the economic threat from China.

“Not only will this result in the further loss of jobs and expertise; it may also mean the loss of companies with long histories of technological excellence and contributions to local communities.”

Mr Kynge said Chinese companies were winning because the country’s huge domestic market gave them greater economies of scale. China also boasted world-class universities, cutting-edge technological innovation and generous state subsidies.

He warned that British companies were losing market share to Chinese rivals not only at home in the UK, but also in China and in other countries where they competed.

“Chinese competitors are going global and rising to the forefront of global technology. That means that a UK business anywhere in the world is going to experience blowback from these uber-competitors coming out of China,” he said.

The soaring cost of energy is hindering British industry’s ability to compete and last week Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical companies warned of “a slow agony of decline” in the face of China’s growing dominance.

The Chatham House report found that in the pharmaceutical sector, China could rip through the clinical development of new drugs at three times the pace of Europe, for half the cost.

Mr Kynge said British and European pharmaceutical firms were now getting Chinese players to develop drugs for them. “They are outsourcing their brains to China. The collateral damage will be an atrophication of the UK’s own ability to innovate in drugs in the future,” he said.

The report also looked at China’s increasing takeover of industries such as wind turbines, machine tools and cars, where Europe until recently still held the upper hand.

The EU is reportedly about to launch new measures to protect its industries from cut-price Chinese imports. But Britain has remained more open to Chinese trade.

‘We need to do a reverse-China on China’

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, told The Telegraph this month that “if you put trade protections up, you’ve got to understand that they’ll probably be reciprocated and you’ll lose out”.

Britain had a £52.5bn deficit in its goods trade with China in the 12 months to the end of March. Goods exports to China declined 0.5pc to £18.5bn, while imports rose 2.4pc to £71bn.

Mr Kynge said the Government needed to reduce the regulatory burden and speed up bureaucratic processes to help British companies compete. Britain also needed to build more infrastructure, and increase the tech skills of its workforce.

Britain should welcome Chinese investment in non-sensitive sectors, he added, as long as the investors transferred technology, used local suppliers or hired and trained British workers.

“These were the conditions of entry for many of the European companies that went to China in the early days – you had to transfer technology. So we need to do a reverse-China on China,” he said.

data.title: Healey splits from Burnham over Heathrow third runway
data.description:
John Healey has insisted a third runway at Heathrow Airport will turbocharge the economy, despite the Prime Minister refusing to back the plan.

The Chancellor said expanding Europe’s second-busiest airport had “always been a case for growth”.

By contrast, Andy Burnham has explicitly declined to endorse a third runway, raising the prospect of a Cabinet split with No 10.

Speaking at the International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, Mr Healey said: “In recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, they have been a big part of jobs and growth.

“And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth.”

The Prime Minister refused to say whether he backed the project after it emerged that the expansion of the London airport could be delayed by up to four years.

Mr Burnham opposed Heathrow expansion as Manchester’s mayor, arguing that the project would delay investment in transport for the North.

He has since said he is “open-minded” about the scheme but that it is a “contested issue” and principally a matter for Londoners.

Some of Mr Burnham’s inner circle is understood to be sceptical about whether the £33bn expansion would deliver on promises to unlock more than 100,000 jobs across the UK.

Opinions are also divided within the Cabinet. Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, has long contested the project on environmental grounds, while Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, has argued it is “incompatible with our legally binding climate agreements”.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, believes that a third runway can only go ahead if it meets Britain’s climate objectives and concerns about noise pollution are dealt with.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, and Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, are among the most enthusiastic supporters of the project.

Louise Haigh, who as First Secretary of State is now Mr Burnham’s de facto deputy, cautiously supported a third runway while she was transport secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, though she insisted it would have to “meet our carbon targets”.

The Government has closed its consultation on the proposals, but has yet to set out the next steps for building a third runway.

Mr Healey said: “The formal position now is that the consultation is closed, led by the transport department. We’re reviewing those, and then further announcements will follow.”

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, had championed the runway to boost the economy, with a target opening date of 2035.

However, Heathrow has now indicated that it may not be operational until 2039.

Thomas Woldbye, Heathrow’s chief executive, is said to be concerned that its investors may not back the project unless it receives approval by the end of the year.

A government source insisted the Prime Minister was “open minded” about the project, adding that it was not unreasonable to “kick the tyres on a massive and tricky commitment you inherited”.

Ms Alexander has also sought to reassure the aviation industry that the Government remains committed to expansion.

Speaking this week, Ms Alexander said that she sees “it as an opportunity to see through what we started”, including “expansion plans for airports”.

Ms Alexander added: “I am as determined as ever to work with you on the Prime Minister’s vision. Make no mistake, when Andy talks about restoring hope and belief, about a Britain re-industrialised, about growth in every postcode, airports are front and centre of that vision.”

A spokesman for British Airways owner IAG said: “We back a third runway at Heathrow because it will create jobs, boost UK regional as well as international connections and keep Britain competitive, provided it is delivered affordably so passengers are not hit with soaring airport charges.”

BA has also suggested that the Government should consider taking a stake in Heathrow or the runway to help keep costs under control.

data.title: Burnham wants to revive British industry. This is why he’ll fail
data.description:
A giant crane slowly eats its way through vast, derelict buildings at the Llanwern steelworks.

At its peak, the site on the outskirts of Newport was a crucial cog in one of the biggest industrial hubs in the world.

Now, workers can only watch as the complex is torn apart.

“We’re literally watching as the place we work is destroyed in front of us,” says one veteran employee.

The facility, owned by Indian conglomerate Tata, produces galvanised steel today but its role has been dramatically reduced over time.

More recently, the steelworks has been threatened by high energy costs and an influx of cheaper, foreign steel that has followed a loosening of tariff restrictions.

As of August, it was only operating at half capacity with hundreds of jobs feared to be at risk.

“It feels like a perfect storm,” frets the employee.

Further along the Welsh coast, in Port Talbot, Tata has also cut some 2,000 jobs as part of plans to close its historic blast furnaces.

These struggles – and those of Britain’s wider steel industry – are among the most visceral examples of the UK’s fading industrial power.

Domestic businesses in carmaking, chemicals and other sectors are struggling to compete with global rivals.

But at Labour’s annual conference last week, Andy Burnham and John Healey vowed to buck this trend with a “new era of industrialisation”.

They have talked up manufacturing, arguing it is vital for national security in an age of instability, winning a rapturous reception from the party faithful.

But what does it mean in practice? And is it just a ridiculous fantasy?

Stephen Phipson, chief executive of manufacturing body Make UK, warns that far from a resurgence, industry is facing threats from “every direction”.

“Reindustrialisation won’t be delivered through speeches, strategies or slogans from Whitehall,” he says.

“It will be delivered by thousands of individual businesses making decisions to recruit, invest and expand.

“And right now too many of those decisions are being postponed.”

Car crash

In the 19th century, Britain was at the heart of the industrial revolution that unleashed an era of breakneck economic growth.

But in the post-war period, the nation’s industrial muscles have gradually atrophied as the global economy’s centre of gravity has shifted.

In the 1970s manufacturing made up around 30pc of all jobs domestically. Since then, that has dwindled to just 7.8pc of workers.

The dramatic decline has transformed once-bustling industrial towns into hotspots of joblessness after major employers shut their factories and moved overseas.

Now, some are worried Healey’s pledge to usher in “a new age of industrialisation” risks harking back to a bygone era.

Reindustrialisation would need to reverse a trend “that has been going on for decades”, says Paul Johnson, the former director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, when “actually, our strength is as a service-based economy”.

The data reflect just that. Last year manufacturing made up 8.3pc of total UK economic output (GVA), compared to an 81pc contribution from the services sector.

As the fortunes of the country’s manufacturers started to turn in the Eighties, a rare bright spot for the sector was Margaret Thatcher’s successful lobbying to bring in Japanese car manufacturers, with Nissan opening its first UK factory in Sunderland in 1984.

But China’s emergence as a manufacturing superpower has put further pressure on British industry since then, along with skills shortages and soaring energy costs.

Today, even Nissan’s highly efficient Sunderland plant has been reduced to running at 50pc capacity.

Top executives have blamed rising costs as a key reason for the idleness, warning that the plant “pays more for electricity than any other Nissan plant in the world”.

“Ultimately, the UK is not a competitive place to be building cars today,” said Alan Johnson, a senior vice president for manufacturing at Nissan, in a parliamentary hearing last year.

There are few signs that the decline is slowing. Stellantis closed its historic Vauxhall plant in Luton last year, putting around 1,000 jobs at risk. Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) – Britain’s biggest domestic car maker – is cutting 4,000 jobs over the next two years as it struggles with tariffs and tough competition overseas.

Against this backdrop, ministers have been courting Chinese brands such as BYD, Jaecoo owner Chery and SAIC Motor, the owner of MG, in the hope they will invest.

But industry sources say even they are wary about the costs of doing business in Britain. Meanwhile, western brands fear the Chinese will undercut them on price – partly thanks to state support from Beijing.

It has prompted questions of whether Britain should embrace China’s carmakers fully or follow the European Union and impose tariffs to protect domestic industry – a demand Brussels has reportedly made a condition of any deal on its “Made in Europe” supply chain standards.

Corroded chemicals sector

But automotive is just one area where competition from China has dramatically altered the landscape.

Since China transformed itself into an export powerhouse and joined the World Trade Organisation in 2001, the UK, like many western economies, has failed to keep up with the influx of cheap imports, leaving many domestic manufacturing companies falling behind.

British petrochemicals tycoon Sir Jim Ratcliffe warned last month that China was “overbuilding” factory capacity for polyvinyl chloride (PVC) – used in sanitation, healthcare, construction and food packaging – and then “dumping” the excess output on Europe.

“The result is an accelerating rate of closure of our chemical industry,” said Sir Jim, whose company Ineos has filed an official complaint with Europe’s competition regulators.

Chemicals used to be the crown jewel of UK industry. But bosses have since found themselves issuing desperate warnings to the Government amid a wave of factory closures – 25 and counting since 2021.

This has been accompanied by a collapse in the sector’s output, falling 60pc over the same period, according to the Chemical Industries Association.

Some economists have nevertheless suggested the flow of ultra-cheap Chinese goods is ultimately to Europe’s benefit.

But Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform, warns the West’s “dangerous” dependency on imports is one of the main reasons policymakers in the US and Europe are pushing for reindustrialisation – with Beijing seen as a far from benevolent trading partner.

“There is a deeper geostrategic rationale underlying the desire to reindustrialise,” Tordoir adds.

Unlike the UK’s car manufacturers, a number of other industries have survived and even kept growing.

“We have a very strong pharmaceutical base and a broader life sciences industry that isn’t likely to go anywhere any time soon, in part because it’s so research and development-intensive,” says Liam Sides, director at Oxford Economics.

The defence sector and aerospace engineering are also held up as parts of UK manufacturing that are growing significantly thanks to new advancements.

Yet for many other companies the question remains: will Burnham’s plan to boost industry really work, or are they stuck on a path to irrelevance?

A new age of industrialisation

As thousands of Labour apparatchiks mingled at the party’s annual conference last week, the merchandise shop in Liverpool was stuffed with memorabilia commemorating former leader Harold Wilson.

It has been 60 years since Wilson’s second election victory in 1966 – and 63 since he vowed to reforge British industry in the “white heat” of technology.

The plan ultimately rested on a sweeping, state-led reorganisation of manufacturing that created behemoths including carmaker British Leyland, the General Electric Company (GEC) and International Computers Ltd, which collectively employed more than half a million people.

Yet Wilson’s policy is now largely viewed as having failed on its own terms.

The boost to economic growth he hoped it would deliver never turned up, while all three of the big companies created through government-orchestrated mergers had gone bust or been broken up 40 years later.

Meanwhile, the Government’s shaky finances in the face of global headwinds also put a ceiling on Wilson’s ambitions – forcing him into a humiliating devaluation of the pound in 1967.

Much of the British state’s involvement in industry was then unwound under Thatcher in the Eighties with the privatisation of businesses including British Aerospace, British Telecom, British Gas, British Airways, Rolls-Royce and British Steel.

Ironically, however, Burnham and Healey, his Chancellor, are now pushing for the Government to resume a more muscular role in a “new era of industrialisation”.

In his Labour conference speech, Healey gave a nostalgic account of the “industrial heartlands” that once powered Britain’s economy while stressing that some sources of employment, such as coal-mining, were “not coming back”.

Instead the Chancellor chose to channel Wilson with an argument that manufacturing had to be “remade for the modern world”. He has also set out plans for the Government to stimulate demand by “buying British”.

“This is the new age of industrialisation,” he told delegates. “Don’t tell me it’s not possible.”

Burnham similarly argued that Britain should seek to lead the world in the deployment and regulation of AI, while name-checking Gordon Brown’s proposal for an “innovation nation” that supports start-ups.

“We led the world first’s industrial revolution from the Midlands and the North of England,” Burnham said. “So why can’t we lead the next?”

As critics have pointed out however, the plan for reindustrialisation so far looks somewhat scattershot.

The most expensive announcement was £6bn for domestic shipbuilders to construct new floating submarine docks – important infrastructure, no doubt, but hardly the technologies of the future.

There are also signs of a mismatch between what ministers are pitching and the more sweeping ambitions of Labour’s union backers.

Unite, the GMB, Unison, the RMT, the Communication Workers Union and the Trades Union Congress have variously called for the nationalisation of the energy, water, transport, postal, telecoms, shipbuilding and steel sectors.

“If they pull it off, reindustrialisation should mean reinvigorating the working-class communities and industrial heartlands of the UK,” says Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the GMB’s national officer for manufacturing.

“It means apprenticeship opportunities for kids that can’t go to university and communities like Scunthorpe, where I’m from, thriving rather than just managing decline.”

She believes the decline of British industry since the Eighties is proof that privatisation hasn’t worked, leaving “foreign entities owning some of our most strategically important industries”.

However, nationalising more of the economy could initially cost the Government hundreds of billions of pounds – and risk saddling taxpayers with huge losses if the investments go bad.

A decision to nationalise British Steel, for instance, is already proving costly, with accounts showing the struggling business is losing almost £700,000 a day.

Turning the situation around will require time, commitment and hefty investments, says Gareth Stace, director general of lobby group UK Steel, as well as a decision on when to close the last blast furnaces in Scunthorpe and replace them with newer electric arc furnaces.

The Government has committed £2.5bn to the steel sector and on Tuesday Blair McDougall, the steel minister, said officials viewed it as “important for our national security”.

“There will be difficult decisions ahead,” he told attendees at an industry drinks reception.

“But our commitment… is to make sure that we do move on... that we do invest, and that we take those decisions we need to take to make sure this is a profitable, resilient and again world-class industry.”

Yet again, there is ambiguity about what Labour wants to achieve.

Last month, MPs on the public accounts committee said the Government had so far failed to set out a plan for British Steel beyond simply “propping up” the business.

One model for success that ministers have pointed to is a cluster of businesses that have based themselves in South Yorkshire.

There, the focus of the economy has moved from coal-mining to high-tech manufacturing with top businesses including Rolls-Royce, Boeing and McLaren now located in a business park built on top of the former Orgreave pit.

This is also where the University of Sheffield opened the Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre (AMRC) in 2004, aiming to bring together academics and companies to develop cutting-edge production techniques.

Chris Read, head of Rotherham city council, says these partnerships are the bedrock of the AMRC’s success.

“None of those partners on their own would have been able to do it,” he says, adding that “kids who live in my borough can now get apprenticeships with companies they’d never be able to work for otherwise” in industries such as clean energy.

But he also believes the era where “you’d have tens of thousands of men” working in traditional industries is probably gone – even as crises including Covid and Donald Trump’s trade wars provide a case for boosting domestic production.

Ministers claim they’re on the same page. Last week, Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, insisted the Government wanted to focus on “future-facing” technologies.

He also said the state wanted to play a more active role supporting innovation, using data to proactively identify businesses that deserve investment from the British Business Bank.

A source close to Reynolds disputes suggestions that the Government’s plan lacks substance, arguing that Labour stands by the “industrial strategy” ministers published under Sir Keir Starmer in summer 2025.

Yet businesses say that document did not go far enough and was sparse on detail, pointing out that Burnham’s promised “10-year plan” for Britain may also diverge from it in significant ways.

In the resulting vacuum, some of Labour’s biggest beasts are jostling for influence. Gordon Brown will gather business titans in Manchester next week for a conference to discuss his “innovation nation” idea, while Sir Tony Blair is calling for the rapid embrace of AI.

Like Wilson, Burnham has vowed to make sure Britain helps to steer the coming technological revolution instead of being swept up by it.

But experts warn there is another, less comfortable parallel between the two leaders: namely that Burnham’s promises depend on forces that are not all under his control.

Eye-watering energy costs

On the banks of the Humber in Hull, the sprawling Saltend chemicals park has been a vital hub of manufacturing for more than a century.

Yet in recent weeks, three factories there have fallen silent – potentially putting some 4,000 jobs at risk.

Ineos, the owner, has laid the blame on one of the Government’s biggest headaches: Britain’s soaring energy costs.

“I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe,” said Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the founder of Ineos.

“But with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and eight times that of China, we just cannot compete.”

It isn’t just gas, either. Across the board, British businesses electricity prices have reached crippling levels.

Official statistics published have previously shown that industrial businesses in Britain faced higher power costs than those in any other developed country.

Separate data from the International Energy Agency also show wholesale electricity prices in the UK have been nearly 200pc higher than the US, 45pc higher than Japan and 41pc higher than France over the past year.

This is a particularly potent threat because cheap electricity is needed to operate many of the “future-facing” industries ministers want to cultivate, from electric arc-forged steel to battery production and electric vehicle manufacturing, says the CER’s Tordoir.

He believes the correct approach is for the UK and European governments to provide targeted support to promising areas, for instance Britain’s semiconductor and aerospace sectors.

Others are more sceptical that Labour’s focus on industry is the right approach, however.

Sides, at Oxford Economics, warned last week: “I personally cannot think of an advanced economy less suited for an industrial resurgence.”

Simon French, chief economist at Panmure Liberum, also warns there will be “no reindustrialisation” unless Labour can improve the country’s economic fundamentals more broadly, including the costs of energy, capital, construction, and employment.

Many businesses complain Starmer and now Burnham are doing the opposite – raising taxes and imposing onerous employment laws and regulations.

“If you don’t get the pre-conditions for economic growth right, no amount of industrial planning will get over that,” French says.

Any attempt by ministers to focus on specific sectors or companies, rather than fix these basic foundations, “will fail miserably”, he adds.

Former IFS boss Johnson is similarly sceptical of the focus on manufacturing specifically.

“A growth strategy is a growth strategy for the economy as a whole, rather than for metal bashing,” he says.

He argues that the nation’s convoluted planning rules and building regulations are hampering investment and making it harder for businesses to expand.

Andrew Sentance, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, also believes the plan for reindustrialisation risks “heading in the wrong direction” and that Britain would be better off focusing on the “knowledge industries” that it excels at today.

“There was a time when manufacturing was the third of our economy back in the Sixties,” he says.

“But we can’t pretend we’re still in that world.”

Businesses are nevertheless lobbying hard for relief. The Confederation of British Industry, will warn next week that British companies are paying 45pc more to power their businesses than those in other rich nations.

Research by Britain’s biggest business group will show that energy bills have doubled.

Time to deliver

Phipson, of Make UK, also warns that before ministers can reindustrialise Britain, they must “first stop making it more expensive to manufacture here”.

“The autumn Budget therefore presents a simple test.”

Yet that is a big ask as Healey prepares for a difficult Budget on Oct 28.

According to economists, the war in the Middle East has blown a £10bn hole in the public finances that the Chancellor will have to plug to keep the bond markets happy. 

He has already warned Labour delegates in Liverpool that “the money New Labour had in the Nineties is simply not there now”.

It raises further questions about whether Burnham can afford to back up his Government’s soaring rhetoric on reindustrialisation with action.

But a failure to meet his party’s expectations will carry its own costs ahead of the next general election, warns the GMB’s Brumpton-Childs.

“If they don’t follow through on what they’ve promised, then it’ll be electoral suicide,” she says.

“The most important thing about hope is delivering, isn’t it?”

Back in Llanwern, the stakes feel all too real for the workers whose jobs are on the line.

Here, Labour’s promises to revive the steel industry have gone down well. But there are real doubts about whether a plan will materialise in time.

“You don’t want to sound too blue about everything,” says the veteran worker. “But it feels like we’ve got some tough times ahead before anything starts improving.”

data.title: Lotus halves British workforce after Trump tariff blow
data.description:
Lotus has cut its UK workforce by more than half after Donald Trump’s tariffs triggered a collapse in sales.

The sports car manufacturer had 600 employees at the end of last year, less than half the 1,300 staff it had before US import duties stunted demand in its biggest market.

The workforce cuts, revealed in newly published accounts, appear to go deeper than Lotus indicated in August last year, when it planned to let go of 550 staff.

Sales at the carmaker – which is based in Hethel, Norfolk – fell 71pc to just 1,539 vehicles in 2025 after the US president raised tariffs on British vehicle imports by 25pc.

While the levy was later reduced after ministers reached a deal with Washington, deliveries in the first half of 2026 remained flat at 896 cars.

Lotus – founded in 1952 by Colin Chapman, an engineer – said it had been forced to cut production as “global tariff uncertainty and evolving trade conditions” hit demand for British sports cars. Lotus’s full-year losses climbed more than 90pc to £263m.

The carmaker, which is owned by China’s Geely, said: “The imposition of 25pc tariffs by the US government in the early part of the year led to a significant reduction in orders from dealers and consumers in Lotus’s largest single market.

“Although tariffs for UK manufacturers were subsequently reduced to 10pc, the introduction of a 100,000-unit quota at this rate has constrained market potential.”

It added that the US tariffs, combined with “softer global demand” across other key markets, had “necessitated the careful alignment of production levels with distributor requirements”.

Lotus Cars, as the UK business is known, was combined in August with Lotus Technology, a Chinese offshoot created after the marque was taken over by Geely in 2017.

The UK business shipped 1pc more cars in the first six months of this year, mostly petrol-engined Emiras priced at between £80,000 and £125,000.

The Chinese business, which makes electric saloon cars and SUVs largely for the domestic market, lifted deliveries 57pc to 3,008.

The imbalance will add to concerns about the future of the Hethel plant after reports last year that Geely, which also owns Sweden’s Volvo, was considering moving production to the US to escape American tariffs.

After the rumours, Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, held emergency talks with Geely, which denied that there were plans to close the plant.

Qingfeng Feng, the chief executive of Lotus, said in August that the expansion of the company’s China-made “lifestyle brands” was part of plans to shift Lotus’s product mix away from traditional sports cars.

However, he said Lotus remained committed to producing British sporting models – including a proposed 1,000-horsepower Type 135 hybrid supercar.

data.title: ‘Del Boy billionaire’ enters race for Poundland
data.description:
A British businessman nicknamed the “Del Boy billionaire” has joined the race to acquire struggling Poundland.

Chris Dawson, the 74-year-old Plymouth-born entrepreneur, is understood to be looking to purchase a selection of the discount retailer’s stores, according to The Times.

The founder of CDS Superstores, which owns The Range, Wilko and Homebase, is among a raft of suitors expressing interest in the budget retailer, which has been put up for sale by owner Gordon Brothers.

The US-based investment company acquired Poundland for £1 last summer as the retailer faced rising operational costs, fierce competition, and a consumer shift toward online shopping.

However, the decision to put it up for sale so soon after the takeover has raised fears that Poundland could be broken up or tipped into administration, putting jobs at risk.

Union officials at Usdaw, who are understood to have been offered a meeting with Poundland management, fear that owner Gordon Brothers may favour selling the business piecemeal.

Poundland has stressed its preference to sell the chain to Irish firm Martin Property Group, which holds real-estate interests spanning shopping centres to hotels.

Although no formal management buyout has been launched, Martin Property Group is backing interest led by Barry Williams, Poundland’s chief executive, and Andy Bond, its director. The firm is proposing a solvent acquisition and working with the board on a potential deal. It could be finalised as soon as this week.

However, bidders continue to circle in case talks falter.

Mr Dawson gained the nickname the “Del Boy billionaire” in the press as a reference to his yellow Lamborghini Urus, which has a personalised number plate “DE11 BOY”, a homage to the character Del Boy Trotter from Only Fools and Horses.

Like Del Boy, the businessman started his career as a market trader, before founding The Range and scaling it to a UK high street giant. He has since purchased both Wilko and Homebase out of administration.

A CDS spokesman said: “We don’t comment on market speculation. Our focus remains on growing our family of brands and delivering outstanding value for customers.”

Poundland has also attracted interest from turnaround firm Modella Capital, which owns WH Smith’s former high street shops, as well as discount supermarket chains Aldi and Lidl, which are understood to be eyeing a selection of UK stores.

Irish family business Henderson Property Group has also expressed interest, further stoking fears that Poundland could be broken up.

A spokesperson for Poundland said: “We understand these kinds of sale processes often lead to significant concern and speculation – much of it wide of the mark.

“We have always had an open door to Usdaw and they know we’re focused on the recovery that’s now firmly embedded in the business.”

Gordon Brothers was contacted for comment.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Scrap ‘delusional’ electric car sales targets, Renault boss says
data.description:
The carmaker behind one of Britain’s most popular electric vehicles (EVs) has urged ministers to scale back “delusional” net zero targets amid fears they risk backfiring.

Adam Wood, the boss of Renault UK, insisted the French automotive giant supported the green transition and pointed to booming sales of the Renault 5 electric hatchback as proof that consumers would buy affordable cars.

However, he warned that the trajectory of the Government’s zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate was so steep that it was becoming “unsustainable” and could force manufacturers to scale back investment in EV technologies.

Speaking at the company’s office in north-west London, Mr Wood told The Telegraph: “For us, the debate is not the destination – we are absolutely convinced the destination is 100pc electric.

“The debate is about the speed at which we get there.

“But we shouldn’t be complacent or delusional that we have something today that is absolutely aligned with the ZEV mandate because we don’t.”

Mr Wood said consumer demand had “not kept pace with the ZEV mandate” and was being propped up by “unsustainable levels” of discounting by manufacturers.

He added: “The trajectory needs to be sustainable for the industry at a time when, let’s not forget, manufacturers are having to invest more than ever in the next generation of technology to make that transition happen.

“Anything that puts in jeopardy that investment – and the certainty that the automotive industry needs more than ever – is unhelpful.”

Ministers are reviewing the ZEV mandate following intense lobbying by carmakers, who say they are struggling to keep up.

Renault’s call to relax the rules will sound alarm bells in Whitehall because the company is one of the few that has managed to stay ahead of the targets.

This year’s headline requirement is for 33pc of cars sold to be electric.

Mr Wood said the French manufacturer’s sales are “approaching 50pc” thanks to the success of the revamped Renault 5. That compares with an overall market share of 26pc for electric cars so far this year.

At the same time, Renault has seen a “seismic” jump in EV sales since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which has sent petrol and diesel prices soaring to record highs, Mr Wood said.

“People are doing the maths,” he said, pointing to analysis showing electric drivers could save £600 a year on fuel.

However, the ZEV mandate target will rise to 38pc of vehicle output in 2027, 52pc in 2028, 66pc in 2029 and 80pc in 2030. Mr Wood said even Renault was worried about meeting it in later years.

He pointed to ongoing driver concerns about the cost and extensiveness of public charging networks, adding: “You’ve got to have an eye on the future because 50pc today is not 80pc in 2030.”

He added that the escalating requirements of the ZEV mandate were not on a “linear curve – it’s an exponential one”.

“We’ve started to demonstrate that when you create a virtuous circle of affordability – accessible vehicles, improving charging infrastructure and a cost of ownership equation which works for people – then you can convert more people to go electric,” he said. “But that doesn’t mean that with a market at 26pc today, we’re on course sustainably to be at 80pc by 2030.”

The targets for electric light commercial vans (LCVs) were particularly challenging, he said.

“The LCV market today is hovering around 10pc for EVs but we’re talking about 70pc by 2030.”

Mr Wood argued that the Renault 5 – which comes in a striking shade of yellow by default – had been successful because it “brought electric cars into a more affordable space” while also “bringing a smile to people’s faces”.

Unlike many other EVs launched by Western brands, it is a small car rather than an SUV, putting it squarely up against the likes of Chinese competitors such as the BYD Dolphin.

“I think the industry, perhaps in pursuit of electrification, has sometimes been guilty of potentially trying to sell a category of vehicles to customers,” Mr Wood said.

“What we’ve come back to is the core of what motivates people to buy. It’s not simply a rational choice, it’s one that’s also emotional.”

The four-door hatchback, which sells for as little as £21,495 after a government grant, was the UK’s most popular EV in April and July this year.

Since its launch in January 2025, almost 20,000 have been sold in the UK, including 10,000 so far this year.

It has helped Renault to grow sales in 2026 while rivals including Ford, Volkswagen and Fiat have flagged.

Mr Wood, a father of two, owns a Renault 5 himself – along with a Renault Scenic SUV – but he admits: “I struggle to prize it away from my wife. They’re great fun to drive.”

Before the end of this year, Renault will also launch the smaller and lower-priced Twingo electric city car for sale in the UK.

It is expected to cost less than £20,000 – or potentially as little as £16,000 after a government grant, should it qualify for the full amount.

That would make it competitive versus even the cheapest cars made by Chinese brands such as BYD and Jaecoo, which have been relentlessly eating into the market shares of Western manufacturers.

“It will be extremely competitive,” Mr Wood said. “The car is really agile and it’s also extremely fun.”

The Twingo was developed in just two years – at “China speed” – because of work carried out by the company’s “advanced China development centre” in Shanghai, where a prototype was built.

Although it was partly designed in China, the vehicle was built on top of a French core design and will be manufactured in Slovenia. The Renault 5 is made in France.

Car development cycles normally take around five years, with Mr Wood arguing that the Twingo’s development was an example of Western carmakers learning how to catch up with their Chinese rivals.

“With Twingo, what we’ve demonstrated is the humility to acknowledge that China is part of the epicentre of global car development, particularly in electric vehicles,” he said.

“That’s what enabled us to break records. We’ve developed a car in two years from concept to reality and brought it to market. Crucially, though, that’s on a platform that was developed in Europe by Renault engineers.

“We’re demonstrating that it is absolutely possible to be competitive [with China]. The Renault 5 is testament to that.”

data.title: Burnham to nationalise Avanti West Coast
data.description:
Avanti West Coast will be nationalised from next year, the Transport Secretary has announced.

Heidi Alexander will use her speech to the Labour Party conference on Monday to outline plans to bring the rail firm into public ownership in March next year, when its contract is expected to expire.

The line, which Andy Burnham uses to travel between London and Manchester, has been beset by frequent delays and cancellations in recent years.

Since the general election two years ago, the Labour Government has been nationalising rail services across the country as contracts have ended.

Nationalisation will be supported by a plan to improve infrastructure, reduce delays and improve passenger experience, the Government said.

Avanti West Coast had the highest proportion of cancellations in Britain this summer at 12.6 per cent – double the national average.

The operator was also worst performing in terms of punctuality, with just 32 per cent of trains arriving on time.

Last month, Avanti drivers were handed a 3.6 per cent pay rise from the Government after threatening to strike, as well as a £720 bonus if they agree to work a fifth day in a given week.

Mr Burnham was one of those entitled to compensation when his train from Manchester to London was delayed in June, as he travelled south to take up his seat in Parliament before ultimately dethroning Sir Keir Starmer.

‘Passengers, not shareholders, will come first’

In a post on social media on Sunday evening, the Prime Minister wrote: “Enough is enough.

“For years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again.

“So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year.

“That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first. More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right.

“We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”

Ms Alexander said: “For years, we’ve heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price. Enough is enough.”

“This Labour Government is committed to putting essential services back in public hands, connecting people to opportunity and delivering growth in every postcode and this move reflects that commitment,” she added.

“We will also introduce a comprehensive improvement plan, focused on delivering for passengers, not shareholders.”

Andy Mellors, the managing director of Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.

“Together, these improvements have given customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the West Coast and wider rail industry.

“Over the coming months, we’ll work closely with the Government to ensure a seamless transition into public ownership while remaining focused on delivering for our customers and communities.”

data.title: Angela Rayner accused of making housing crisis worse
data.description:
Angela Rayner has been accused of making the property crisis worse after a housebuilder lost its battle to construct hundreds of homes in south-east London.

Berkeley Group had mounted a legal challenge to revive plans to replace Peckham’s derelict 1980s Aylesham Centre with 867 homes, but its appeal was rejected by a judge on Monday.

Ms Rayner’s officials in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) have also frozen a second Berkeley project, for 586 homes, at the redundant Motspur Park gasworks in Kingston.

Rob Perrins, the chief executive of Berkeley Group, warned on Wednesday that the decisions underscored the “gulf between positive planning policies and what actually happens when you try to build homes in London”.

With its projects repeatedly rejected by councils and planning inspectors, Mr Perrins said the housebuilder was increasingly forced to rely on “hugely costly and slow” legal appeals or decisions by ministers to secure approval for developments.

Yet plans for its Motspur Park development were “immediately put on hold by central government” in August, Mr Perrins said, and now must be reviewed by Ms Rayner, despite securing consent from the Mayor of London’s office.

Mr Perrins said: “All of this creates extreme uncertainty and is undermining the Government’s housing agenda.

“Housing delivery in London is at a record low. At a time when we should be fighting to attract investment and build more homes, we’re fighting it off. The result is fewer homes, less growth and a worsening housing crisis.”

In Peckham, the housebuilder had applied to build homes in more than a dozen tower blocks running up to 20 storeys high, served by a new Morrisons supermarket.

But its proposals were rejected by the planning inspectorate in May on heritage grounds, which ruled they were “visually intrusive”.

Mr Perrins described the Peckham saga as a “10-year planning nightmare”, adding that Historic England, the heritage watchdog, had not objected to the plans.

“The outcome is no new investment, no jobs, no homes,” he added. “All the policies support housing, but the decisions block it time and time again.”

The site has been earmarked for housing since 2014. It is estimated the project would generate nearly 1,000 jobs along with £15m for the council to invest in the community.

But local groups protested against the project, including Aylesham Community Action, labelling it “gentrification [on] steroids”. The campaign was backed by Miatta Fahnbulleh, the local Labour MP who was appointed Energy Secretary in July.

Lord Khan , the Mayor of London, meanwhile, called in and approved Berkeley’s Motspur Park development after councillors rejected the proposal in March.

But the Housing Secretary issued a holding direction in August that bars City Hall from officially granting consent, despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to leave more control of building projects to mayors.

Separately on Wednesday, Taylor Wimpey, a competitor to Berkeley, said it had no more plans to build new homes in London and warned the city’s housing market was “fundamentally broken”.

Jennie Daly, the chief executive of Taylor Wimpey, told The Times: “Baseline viability is, I think, fundamentally broken in London.

“The reward for undertaking what is a very high-risk form of development in London has just evaporated.”

A spokesman for the MHCLG said its planning reforms had led to a 298pc increase in new London housing starts compared to a year ago. It is also investing £11.7bn into council housing in the capital.

He added: “We are also backing the Mayor of London and working closely with industry to get more homes built for Londoners – making sure good schemes are not left in limbo while unlocking jobs, growth and opportunity.”

data.title: Nandy’s ‘Netflix tax’ is the purest insanity
data.description:
The news that Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is considering adding a “streamer tax” to her list of options for bolstering the BBC’s finances caused predictable outrage amongst readers of the Daily Telegraph – and no doubt many others.

It is a dumb idea. Indeed, so dumb that I did not bother to address it last month in my article on why a broadband tax or a supplement to council tax were poor alternatives to the licence fee (itself acknowledged by both Ms Nandy and the BBC as no longer fit for purpose).

Apart from being deeply unpopular, a streamer tax would face multiple problems. It could not just be imposed on Netflix, so presumably would also apply to Amazon, Disney+, Apple TV, Hulu, TNT, HBO Max and Paramount.

It does not take a genius to work out that all these services are US-owned. What a vengeful president – still with two years in office remaining – might do in response to what he would undoubtedly perceive as an assault on American entrepreneurs is not hard to imagine. The BBC’s US streaming service (which it values at £700m) might be taxed out of existence. Tariffs on Scotch whisky or UK-made cars might double. This is a fight with no winners.

In any event, the practical difficulties of a streamer tax are considerable. Amazon Prime is essentially a parcel delivery service, with a free video package attached. How do you tax something with no price tag? For millions of customers, their Netflix – or Paramount, or TNT or HBO Max – subscription is wrapped up in their Sky or Virgin Media package, often alongside a broadband offering. So this would be a tax on Sky and cable subscriptions – two more politically influential US-owned businesses.

Millions of people subscribe to more than one of these services. Which one would be required to levy the BBC charge? Would they be allowed to deduct the cost of collecting the fee? Who would decide the amount?

Each of these providers maintains a separate database. How would each provider know that a customer has already paid the BBC fee? Would the law be changed to allow sharing of databases? Where would that leave consumer privacy?

Of course, there are millions of licence-fee holders who do not currently subscribe to any streaming services. What if they now choose to do so? Streamer subscriptions are individual. Television licence fees are paid by households. A household might contain more than one subscriber to a streaming service. Which of them has to pay? Who checks the records?

If a would-be Netflix subscriber tells the company they already pay for the BBC, what is Netflix expected to do? What enforcement mechanisms are envisaged? The BBC’s 220 licence-fee inspectors – notoriously ineffective – would be swamped.

The worst aspect of this bad idea is that it encourages the BBC to believe it is someone else’s job to provide its finances. There is a simple way to replace the licence fee: convert BBC TV to a paid-for streaming service. Only when the BBC learns to stand on its own feet will it be incentivised to tackle its chronic inefficiency, overmanning and top-heavy wage bill. Leave the other streamers be.

David Elstein is a former head of programming at BSkyB and chief executive of Channel 5

data.title: Rejoining single market could give UK a £150bn boost, Goldman Sachs claims
data.description:
Rejoining the EU’s single market could boost the UK’s economy by as much as £150bn, Goldman Sachs has claimed.

The Wall Street bank told clients in a note that there was “significant economic upside from ‘Breturn’” as it backed Andy Burnham’s calls for closer ties with the bloc.

Analysts said that rejoining the single market could grow the economy by between 2pc and 5pc, equivalent to a boost of £61bn to £152bn by the start of the next decade.

Mr Burnham has promised to have a “serious dialogue” about the UK’s relationship with the EU, presenting a summit with Brussels next month as a possible first step to rejoining.

The Prime Minister has said it would be a “major dereliction of duty” not to explore closer relations with the EU. He is likely to seize upon Goldman Sachs’s analysis to bolster his case.

Goldman Sachs donated to the Britain Stronger in Europe campaign in the run-up to the 2016 referendum and warned it would shift jobs to Europe if the UK left. The Wall Street bank employs thousands of people in London.

Andy Haldane, the former chief economist at the Bank of England, has warned that reopening the Brexit debate risked damaging the economy by freezing business investment.

Mr Haldane, who advised Mr Burnham during his campaign to become Prime Minister, told LBC this week: “Could we strike a better deal with the EU? Yes. Would that deliver some growth dividend over some five, 10, 15-year horizons? Probably.

“Do we want to rerun that Brexit referendum? Would that not be a thing that escalated uncertainty and therefore set business back on its heels? I think that is the risk in this. That it opens up a can of worms that generates more uncertainty at a time when stability is needed.”

Goldman Sachs economists acknowledged that closer ties with the EU would be a political decision and said “any reset would require negotiation, political trade-offs and time before benefits materialise”.

They added: “But the economic upside from closer UK-EU relations could be large, supporting our constructive view on the UK’s longer-run growth prospects.”

Options for closer ties range from joining a customs union to full-fat membership. Forming a customs union similar to Turkey’s arrangement would bring an estimated £30bn boost, Goldman Sachs claimed.

The bank claims that Brexit has left the UK economy 6pc smaller than it otherwise would have been, something other economists believe is “tenuous”.

Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “Since 2016, the UK, Germany, France and Italy have all grown at very similar, sluggish rates. The UK has been a little bit stronger than Germany and Italy, and a little bit weaker than France.

“The trouble with this argument is it implies that in the absence of Brexit, the UK would have substantially outperformed the other major European economies.”

Mr Beck highlighted that this suggested that without Brexit, the UK would have grown at a rate more similar to the US, despite feeling a bigger impact from economic shocks and struggling with high energy prices.

“The question then is why, when we were hit harder by the energy price shock, we were hit harder by Covid, we had more severe lockdowns, why would we have had this substantial outperformance?”

data.title: Burnham oversaw £55m taxpayer loan to UAE businesses
data.description:
Andy Burnham oversaw a £55m taxpayer loan to United Arab Emirates-owned businesses while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, The Telegraph can disclose.

The money was awarded to three Jersey-based property companies ultimately controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan, the owner of Manchester City FC.

He is also a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family and vice president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

The decisions to issue the loans were taken in two meetings in 2017, both of which Mr Burnham chaired as mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA).

They are the first pieces of evidence that the Prime Minister was directly involved in decisions that favoured Abu Dhabi. 

Last month Mr Burnham became embroiled in a row over Manchester City after the Premier League found the club guilty of financial irregularities.

The Prime Minister initially said he would be “really concerned” if the UAE decided to sell Manchester City, before rowing back on the comments, with Downing Street insisting that no one was above the rules. 

The UAE is appealing against the decision and has threatened to pull out of major UK investment projects in retaliation against the Premier League’s verdict.

The financing for the property companies came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund (GMHILF), a pot of taxpayers’ money lent to the region by central government on the basis that it would be used to tackle the housing crisis.

The £300m fund was supposed to be lent to private developers to “kickstart housing projects that would otherwise be difficult to fund from elsewhere”, according to a GMCA press release in which Mr Burnham was quoted.

The Prime Minister is likely to face questions over how well GMCA adhered to this brief by authorising the loan of public money to companies controlled by one of the wealthiest men in the world.

Louie French, the shadow sports minister, said: “We need to know why these firms got loans from a fund intended for housing projects that would not otherwise be viable. 

“They could easily have got competitively priced loans on the private market, so why did the taxpayer have to finance them instead, thanks to approval at meetings chaired by Burnham when he was mayor?”

John Leech, the Liberal Democrat chairman of the GMCA overview and scrutiny committee, said: “Clearly, there would be no suggestion that the money couldn’t come from somewhere else in the case of Sheikh Mansour.”

Mr Leech added that the loans appeared out of kilter with the “stated aim” of the funds, and that the committee would look into “this issue of public loans for housing schemes in Greater Manchester”.

The disclosures raise fresh questions about the links between Abu Dhabi and Manchester. Mr Burnham has repeatedly praised the UAE for investment that helped to transform the city, but it has not been clear until now that Sheikh Mansour’s contribution was partly financed by loans from taxpayers’ money.

Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), has repaid the loans with interest. The rate of interest is not known.

Mr Burnham has come under mounting scrutiny for property deals which favoured Abu Dhabi, carried out by Manchester city council.

The Telegraph revealed last week that the council used public money to pay millions of pounds more than its nearest competitor for a dilapidated retail park that it intended to reserve for development by Abu Dhabi.

Mr French said: “Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Man City case was completely extraordinary and totally out of touch. But now it is beginning to make sense. The Prime Minister needs to come clean: why did he let these loans proceed?”

Sources close to Mr Burnham have previously played down his involvement in controversial decisions favouring Abu Dhabi, saying either that they were taken before he became mayor or by Manchester city council, one of the 10 councils that made up his combined authority.

However, GMCA minutes show that he chaired the meeting at which the enormous loans were approved.

The decisions to approve them were taken collectively by GMCA members, rather than by Mr Burnham alone. His office declined to comment, including on whether he raised any objections to the loan. GMCA also declined to comment.

All three loans went to companies that were ultimately owned by ADUG.

Two of the loans, totalling more than £30m, went to New Little Mill Developments Ltd and Vesta Street Developments Ltd. Subsequent filings show that the ultimate beneficiary of the Jersey-based companies was Sheikh Mansour.

According to University of Sheffield research on Manchester city council’s joint venture with ADUG, Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle was also the ultimate beneficiary of the third company, Lampwick Developments Ltd, at the time the GMCA approved a loan to it of £24.5m.

A separate council document, obtained by The Telegraph, states that the money would be used to build 213 apartments on privately owned land that already had planning permission, and that, along with Vesta Street and New Little Mill, was one of three schemes that were “brought forward by Manchester Life”.

Manchester Life is a joint venture between Manchester city council, and ADUG.

‘We will invest it wisely’

The GMCA minutes show that Richard Leese, who was the deputy mayor of the GMCA – who is also a director of the Manchester Life joint venture – recused himself from discussions about the loans.

“Councillor Richard Leese declared a prejudicial interest in this report... and left the room during the discussion of the report,” the September minutes said.

Council documents claim that in addition to the Lampwick apartments, the loans would be used to create 68 apartments at New Little Mill, and 169 apartments and three townhouses at Vesta Street, New Islington.

The money for the GMHILF was provided by central government. The GMCA was entrusted with approving loans from the fund to developers in order to accelerate building projects.

Speaking about the fund after it launched in 2015, Bill Enevoldson, GMCA’s chief investment officer, said: “It is not designed to finance unviable projects but can unlock currently unfundable ones…

“Greater Manchester is in a unique position. This money is at our disposal and we will invest it wisely to help speed up the delivery of much-needed new housing of all types right across the region.”

Developers borrowing money do so on the basis that they will repay it with interest, so that it can be lent out again.

The GMCA must return at least 80 per cent of the pot to central government by April 2028. The pot has been lent more than three times over, delivering 11,000 new homes.

‘Competitive terms offered’

However, an “evaluation report” commissioned by GMCA from analysis firm GC Insight suggests that developers have been attracted to its favourable terms.

They told GC Insight that they had borrowed through the fund “not out of necessity” but owing to “competitive terms offered by the fund, particularly in relation to interest rates, funding limits, and flexibility on loan-value ratios” and because it was perceived to be a “more flexible/understanding lender should progress on the development go awry”.

The terms of the GMHILF loans to the three Abu Dhabi-backed companies have not been made public.

A Manchester Life spokesman stressed that ADUG put its own capital into projects before accessing loans from GMHILF, and that these loans were repayable external debt financing, commonly used by property developers.

The spokesman said: “The £55.7m represented the external debt financing for the three relevant developments. It did not form part of the private-sector equity investment in Manchester Life. Presenting them as though they constituted the investment in Manchester Life materially overstates their role.”

He added that Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle invested more than £160m into the first two phases of the building scheme, and that it could only draw down the GMHILF funds once the the projects had been brought to a certain stage.

He said: “ADUG provided the equity and risk capital required to bring the schemes through planning and design and to the point at which the development-finance facilities became available.”

The Manchester Life spokesman added that it was “not in a position to comment on the objectives, eligibility criteria, approval process or individual lending decisions” of the fund. But he said that Manchester Life completed 453 homes, and that the three loans were all repaid in full with interest.

Lampwick has since been sold to a US investor, although the properties are still marketed by Manchester Life. The Lampwick Developments Ltd which was awarded the loan is unrelated to the UK-based company of the same name.

data.title: Healey warned that tax raid on shops will stoke inflation
data.description:
Retail bosses are to warn John Healey that a tax raid on shops will push up prices and worsen the cost of living crisis.

At a Downing Street summit with supermarket bosses on Tuesday, the Chancellor will be warned that retailers cannot absorb more costs and will pass them on to consumers.

Writing in The Telegraph ahead of the breakfast meeting, Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC), warned that shops “cannot afford more bad decisions”.

Ms Dickinson said: “We will warn Healey that retailers cannot absorb endless costs, which means ordinary shoppers shoulder the burden. Families pay more for their weekly shop. Parents pay more for back-to-school clothing. Students pay more for a phone or laptop.

“It’s jobs, too. Retail employment is at its lowest level on record. Job losses do not just hurt retailers. They mean fewer opportunities for people to enter the workplace, less money earned and spent locally and less growth for communities.”

The Chancellor will meet executives from Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Amazon, Co-op and Marks & Spencer, among others, at the pre-Budget summit. Bosses are expected to caution Mr Healey that business rates, employment taxes and high energy costs are driving up inflation and killing employment.

Labour has enacted a series of tax increases since coming to power in 2024, including a £25bn raid on employers’ National Insurance Contributions that has been blamed for falls in the number of jobs in the retail, wholesale and hospitality industries.

Ms Dickinson, who will attend the summit, said: “Lazy thinking over the last two years has led to higher prices and fewer jobs. This will only get worse if government continues to treat retailers as a purse to be raided.”

HMV announced on Monday that it was closing its flagship Oxford Street shop just three years after reopening it, warning it had become “commercially unsustainable”. Zavvi, the online music and collectables retailer, separately fell into administration.

The warning to Mr Healey comes amid growing tensions between retailers and government ahead of the Budget on Oct 28.

Jason Tarry, the chairman of John Lewis and Waitrose, warned over the weekend that a tax raid on warehouses would trigger a wave of closures. Writing in The Telegraph, he said the mooted policy would “only harm our high streets”.

Mr Healey hastily ruled out an increase in business rates for warehouses in response.

However, the Institute for Fiscal Studies has warned that the Chancellor will need to find £35bn in either tax rises or spending cuts to meet all the commitments made by the Government.

New figures on Tuesday showed that shops suffered a sharp slowdown in sales last month. Sales grew by 1.3pc in September, compared to 2pc in the same month a year earlier. The BRC said the public were “still cautious with their spending ahead of expected rises in household bills and taxes”.

As well as warning against further tax increases, executives will also push the Chancellor to remove levies from energy bills and address the tax loophole that allows online Chinese retailers to sell goods into the UK without paying the same customs duties charged to British businesses.

Industry group UKHospitality, which will also attend the Downing Street meeting, is expected to push the Government to use Brexit freedoms to reduce the sector’s VAT rate to 10pc.

Proposed changes to the system which classifies foods as healthy or unhealthy are also likely to be discussed, amid concerns over the Government’s food strategy.

Tina McKenzie, the national chairman of the Federation of Small Businesses, said: “Ministers say they want growth, but growth does not happen by squeezing margins, making employment more expensive and putting barriers in the way of expansion.”

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Healey should use the meeting to take his boot off the neck of the retail and hospitality sectors.

“Number one should be shelving Labour’s anti-employment laws, followed closely by business rates relief.”

Robert Jenrick, of Reform UK, said an increase in the VAT threshold, an about-turn on National Insurance contributions and the end of the Employment Rights Act would help the economy.

“Small business owners need a government that stops punishing them for employing people and keeping their doors open,” he said.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, will separately meet technology bosses in Downing Street to discuss AI on Tuesday. One technology source attending the gathering said they would be looking for signs that an increase in Capital Gains Tax was off the table and confirmation of no new “dramatic” AI regulations.

Retailers cannot afford more bad decisions

By Helen Dickinson

On Tuesday, I will be meeting the Chancellor with other retail leaders to discuss what the retail industry needs from the Budget. We will be clear: the choices he makes at the end of this month will determine whether more shops open or close, whether retail jobs grow or decline and whether prices rise faster or slower.

The Chancellor wants to breathe new life into our high streets and deliver growth in every postcode. We will tell him that retailers share that ambition, but government policy must help businesses deliver it rather than make it harder.

Our latest consumer polling shows these are exactly the issues people want the Chancellor to focus on. Almost nine in 10 people (89pc) want government to prioritise reducing the cost of living, while 83pc want action on youth unemployment and 77pc say improving Britain’s high streets should be a priority.

The public are spot on. Retailers – and so, it appears, the Government – also want the same things. Our message to the Chancellor will be simple: policy must now match that ambition.

We cannot afford more bad decisions. The 2024 Budget lowered the employer National Insurance contributions threshold and raised the rate, leading to 122,000 retail jobs being lost in two years. The 2025 Budget put embattled high streets under further strain with higher business rates.

The industry tax burden is up 20pc over those two years to £41bn in 2026/27. Put into perspective, that’s almost £3 in taxes for every £4 of profit made – a higher tax burden than any other sector of the economy, alongside hospitality.

We will warn Healey that retailers cannot absorb endless costs, which means ordinary shoppers shoulder the burden. Families pay more for their weekly shop. Parents pay more for back-to-school clothing. Students pay more for a phone or laptop.

It’s jobs, too. Retail employment is at its lowest level on record. Job losses do not just hurt retailers. They mean fewer opportunities for people to enter the workplace, less money earned and spent locally and less growth for communities.

Almost three million people work in retail – a career open to people whatever their qualifications or where they live. One in five people started their career in the industry.

Retailers want to be part of the solution. Last month, more than 40 retailers helped us launch Opening Shift, a BRC-DWP-led initiative to create thousands of work experience placements for those left behind. This is a crucial step towards an industry goal of creating 100,000 paid jobs for Neets (those not in education, employment or training) by 2029.

But on Tuesday we will challenge the Chancellor on a fundamental contradiction: government cannot expect businesses to create more jobs while continually making them more expensive to provide. Lazy thinking over the last two years has led to higher prices and fewer jobs. This will only get worse if government continues to treat retailers as a purse to be raided.

So how do we fix it?

To start, the Chancellor should cut the cost of employing young people by raising the National Insurance threshold to give businesses greater capacity to take people on. He should address the rising cost of running and investing in shops by freezing business rates, which otherwise will rise faster than UK growth, and ending the new surtax that penalises larger stores.

These steps would help deliver exactly what the public wants. A new store creates local jobs and attracts shoppers. Investment in an existing store strengthens a high street and supports surrounding businesses. More people in work means more money earned and spent locally.

This is the central message we will take to the Chancellor on Tuesday: you cannot tax your way to growth by squeezing the businesses expected to deliver it. Giving one of the most highly taxed industries in the UK more room to invest is a route to more jobs, stronger high streets and greater growth.

Retail is committed to playing its part. The public, government and retailers want the same outcome. This Budget is the Government’s opportunity to show that its policies match those ambitions, and make it easier to deliver them, not harder.

Helen Dickinson is chief executive of the British Retail Consortium
