data.title: Ronni Ancona: ‘Trying to give up wine feels like a barren wilderness in front of me’
data.description:
Ronni Ancona, 58, is an actress, comedian, impressionist and writer. Here, for our regular My Saturday column, Ancona shares how she spends her downtime.

8am

I wake up with my 10-year-old black cat, Tommy, literally slapping me around the face with his paws or straddling me, demanding full attention. He then gallops downstairs because he’s the size of a small donkey.

I get out of bed with good intentions that I’m going to start the day with a hot lemon water or a probiotic or whatever I happen to have read about the night before. But it just ends up with me having the same large milky coffee from my old stroppy coffee machine.

10am

During the week I wouldn’t usually have breakfast. Not because I’m fasting, but because I’m disorganised and forgetful. But at a weekend, the gloves are off, so I probably would have toast and marmalade.

If I’m going to go to a café with my daughter, she’s obsessed, as most of her generation is, with mashed avocado and eggs on top and it’ll cost 25 quid. But on some Saturdays, I won’t have breakfast because I know I will be eating a copious amount of food later in the day.

I come from a generation where you’re made to feel ashamed if you don’t achieve anything or do anything in a day, so I’ll be looking up exhibitions and museums that I should go to, but which sold out weeks ago. So I will be cursing organised people.

1pm

Because of the way my brain works during the week, I have lots of tasks and jobs that I’ve constantly shunted towards Saturday. So by the time Saturday arrives, I’m usually facing a mountain of washing, sorting and general domestic collapse. I’m such a people pleaser, so I’ll have cards to send or people to call. I don’t excel at many things in life, but I am an excellent procrastinator. I’ll make lists of things to do. Then I make lists for the list.

I’ll also have one eye on the work I have to do later in the week, whether that’s writing, reading a script ahead of filming, or preparing for a podcast. At the moment, I’m producing a film, so that’s scary and a huge amount of work to do.

3pm

For lunch, I will do a big salad thing. It’s always a bit impulsive. A poor man’s Ottolenghi. Lots of random bits that may not go together. Since the advent of social media, I’ll get so excited by all these little recipes I see on there. I’ll invariably save them. I never know where I’m saving them to, though, so I won’t be able to find them. I always remember the recipes at the last moment, so I’ll end up doing a mutated version where there is a key ingredient that’s missing.

5pm

Even if I don’t have that much to do, I will end up embroiled in my daughter’s plans, taking her to see her friends or providing food for them. Or I’ll consider exercising, then I’ll just end up going for a long walk because I love walking. I try to go to different places in London for a walk. I’ll walk down to Hammersmith and down by the river. Or I’ll go to Hampstead Heath. One of the joys of London is that you can walk places.

I end up sometimes doing a weekly shop on a Saturday. Just because I’ve been so busy, and I have a doctor husband and he’s busy, too. It’s the worst day to go.

7pm

If I’m not doing anything on a Saturday night, I will definitely go with my grumpy doctor husband round the corner to a pub. I’ll have half a lager, we’ll sit outside and have some peanuts, and then come back and make dinner.

I don’t drink during the week unless it’s a special occasion. I’m trying to give up wine but, for me, totally giving up is like a barren wilderness stretching in front of me. I come from a long line of pub owners on my father’s side, so I feel quite sad that a lot of these lovely pubs have gone now.

I also like being able to walk around the corner and then walk back as opposed to facing the Underground on a Saturday night. That’s what puts me off going far away on a Saturday night.

8pm

It’s a mixture of ordering in food and me cooking. I do a lot of very exciting and unusual chicken and salmon dishes. With lots of side dishes. My husband does a very good stir fry and a good omelette. Those are his two main things. But even though I cook the vast majority of stuff, he gets the attention for the stir fry and omelette.

9pm

I’m a flopper on a Saturday night. Unless I’m going out with friends or there’s been a previous arrangement. I’m very happy to just lie there and watch a box set, or snuggle up with the girls and watch a very unchallenging film. I recently adored Hacks. I thought it was phenomenal. I love watching comedy at that level. I thought the writing and their intergenerational relationship was just a joy to watch. We are watching a little German spy espionage show at the moment called Unfamiliar.

11pm

I fell into a terrible habit of mindlessly doomscrolling before I went to sleep. That was a disaster. I just ended up thinking, “I’ve got to do that. I should do that. I should be wearing that. I should be taking that.” It was a morbid fascination and very toxic. I’ve now made sure that I have a book next to my bedside table. Not necessarily a great book, but a page turner. I am going to bed earlier and earlier, because I know that Tommy is going to make a dramatic entrance, splay himself all over the bed like a 1930s diva in the middle of the night, and wake me up.

Ronni Ancona rose to fame in the early 2000s with the comedy sketch show The Big Impression opposite Alistair McGowan, where her impressions of Victoria Beckham, Barbara Windsor and Nigella Lawson earned the show a Bafta TV Award for Best Comedy Programme in 2002. Ancona has also appeared in ITV’s The Sketch Show, Last Tango in Halifax, The Trip To Italy, Skins, Eastenders, and as a panellist on QI and a contestant on Strictly Come Dancing.

She lives in West London with her husband Gerard Hall, a specialist rheumatologist and physician, and their two daughters.

data.title: Richard Branson: Trump is appeasing dictators and autocrats
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson has accused Donald Trump of being “an appeaser to autocrats and dictators”.

The outspoken Virgin Group founder criticised Mr Trump on LinkedIn in response to reports that the US president had blocked Ukraine from the Pentagon’s Starshield system, a critical defensive and battlefield support system.

The British billionaire wrote: “The Trump administration has become an appeaser to autocrats and dictators, putting their personal whims before the best interests of the American people and those of the free world.

“How will America’s allies ever be able to trust this administration again, when they are now turning against them at a time of war and suffering?”

Sir Richard is among just a handful of corporate executives who have been prepared to criticise Mr Trump publicly, and has been escalating his attacks this week.

In a series of posts this week, he criticised both Mr Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and also the US president’s subsequent verbal attacks on Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s leader.

On Monday, he described Mr Trump’s deal with Putin for 1.8 million tonnes of Russian diesel as “the most astonishing act of hypocrisy I’ve seen in my lifetime, and I’ve been around for 76 years”.

Sir Richard claimed the hypocrisy lay in the fact that Mr Trump only last month signed into law a policy that allowed Washington to impose tariffs on other countries that bought Russian or Iranian oil.

He also said the White House’s gradual loss of interest in Ukraine had evolved into “a bloody backstabbing”.

He said on Tuesday that Mr Trump’s comments on Mr Zelensky’s culpability for the war were “beyond belief”. On Thursday, he warned that “the free world” could be “dismantled before our very eyes”.

Sir Richard regularly airs his views on political issues, particularly on climate change. More recently he has advocated closer relations between Britain and the EU.

But he is almost alone among executives in launching such scathing attacks on Mr Trump.

Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan Chase, has occasionally spoken in favour of policies that challenge the White House. He has backed the independence of the US Federal Reserve and recently proposed building “a big, beautiful relationship” with the EU.

Albert Bourla, the boss of Pfizer, has meanwhile criticised the views of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on vaccinations.

But few directly attack Mr Trump’s decisions for fear of retribution.

Chrystia Freeland, the former Canadian deputy prime minister, wrote in the Financial Times on Friday that if Mr Trump suffered defeat in the Nov 3 midterms, it could trigger more open attacks on him from Wall Street corporate titans.

She wrote: “I have had more than a dozen conversations with US CEOs who have apologised to me for their president’s conduct and told me he is hurting America and the world.”

She said many still feared being punished for speaking out but were now poised to move with the herd. 

“Trump’s naked betrayal of Ukraine and open support for Putin could be the last straw,” she said.

The White House was contacted for comment.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Healey urged to cut stamp duty on new homes to reap £4bn windfall
data.description:
John Healey has been urged to cut stamp duty on newly built homes in a move that one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders estimates could hand the Treasury a £4.2bn windfall.

In its Budget submission, Berkeley Group told the Chancellor that cutting the levy could revive a market that it warned was “sliding over an economic cliff edge”.

In the submission, seen by The Telegraph, the listed property developer called for stamp duty to be capped at 1pc for first-time buyers and downsizers.

It also urged Mr Healey to scrap a 5pc surcharge levied on investors in new-build rental homes.

The housebuilder estimated that the package could deliver an extra 60,000 homes per year.

Rob Perrins, the executive chairman of Berkeley, said: “Our position has always been that a stamp duty reduction on new-builds – especially around the investor surcharge, first-time buyers and downsizers – is the best and quickest lever.

“This is still needed alongside Your First Home to restart homebuilding in urban areas.”

The intervention came after Andy Burnham unveiled Your First Home, an equity loan scheme aimed at assisting more young people on to the housing ladder.

Designed as a scaled-back version of the previous Help to Buy initiative, the policy will be open to first-time buyers with a 2.5pc deposit, with backing from a 20pc equity loan from the Government.

Mr Healey is expected to formally launch the new policy in the Budget later this month.

However, Berkeley’s submission suggested the scheme would not be enough to solve an “acute crisis, particularly in London”.

The Treasury also reportedly rejected calls for a stamp duty break for downsizing homebuyers earlier this month.

Berkeley argued that higher interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty and rising taxes had led to a “significant slowdown in the rate of new housing sales”.

Only 8,840 private homes were sold in the capital last year, according to the document, down 56pc since 2022.

The housebuilder acknowledged that a cap for first-time buyers could cost the Treasury money, but argued this would be more than offset by extra revenue for the public purse from investors and buyers downsizing.

Berkeley calculated that removing the 5pc investor surcharge would save the typical investor around £13,000, meaning sales would need to rise by just 7pc for the Treasury to break even.

Using figures from the Office for Budget Responsibility, Berkeley estimated that scrapping the charge would unlock sales growth of at least 30pc, providing £4.2bn to the Exchequer.

The housebuilder added that a cap for those moving to a smaller home would probably be even “more lucrative for the Treasury”.

While older homeowners would pay less stamp duty on their own purchase, each move would trigger a chain of moves involving transactions that attract the full amount.

Outside stamp duty, each newly built home is thought to produce around £49,800 in taxes, such as corporation tax and the building safety levy.

Berkeley said: “If the Government wants to increase housing supply as measured against its high-profile commitment to deliver 1.5 million homes this Parliament, there are few policy measures available with the potential to deliver such an immediate impact, whilst sticking to a tight fiscal envelope.”

The Government has been contacted for comment.

data.title: Unions fear Poundland will go into administration ‘within days’
data.description:
Poundland could be pushed into administration within days, putting 12,000 jobs at risk, one of Britain’s largest trade unions has claimed.

Usdaw, which represents 370,000 retail workers, said it feared that owners Gordon Brothers could decide the fate of the discount retailer as soon as Tuesday.

Poundland is subject to a number of competing bids after Gordon Brothers decided to sell the business but unions say they have “deep concerns” that it will be pushed into administration.

Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said the union has repeatedly requested urgent talks with Gordon Brothers since rumours first surfaced that the private equity firm intended to sell.

“Sources within the company are telling me that a decision about the future of Poundland could be made as early as [Tuesday], and there are deep concerns that the business could go into administration, which would be a disaster for our members,” Mr Auluk said.

“We are aware that a management buyout has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down. We found it difficult to understand why Poundland was being described as struggling, after the company recently announced they had returned to like-for-like sales growth and staff were being thanked for their ‘amazing efforts’.”

Gordon Brothers is pursuing a sale process for the group and has received expressions of interest from a number of parties.

These include turnaround firm Modella Capital and a deal backed by Barry Williams, Poundland’s current boss, and Andy Bond, its former chairman.

Henderson Property Group, an Irish family business, has also expressed an interest, raising fears that Poundland could be broken up.

Additionally, discount grocers Aldi and Lidl are understood to also be interested in a number of UK stores.

Martin Property Group, which holds real estate interests ranging from shopping centres to hotels, has proposed a solvent acquisition of the business.

This is the group backing Mr Williams’ interest in acquiring the group although is it understood that no formal “management buyout” has been launched.

Union officials, who are understood to have been offered a meeting with Poundland’s management, fear Gordon Brothers may favour selling the business piecemeal to supermarket chains.

Gordon Brothers acquired Poundland little more than a year ago and oversaw a store closure programme to restructure the business.

The private equity firm is now reportedly demanding full repayment of a £30m shareholder loan, which it acquired for just £1 as part of its original buyout, from any potential buyer.

Gordon Brothers could leverage this debt to trigger an administration process if a full-company sale is not reached.

Despite recent restructuring, Poundland remains one of the largest general merchandise retailers in the UK.

A Poundland spokesman said: “We confirm that Barry Williams, Andy Bond and the Poundland leadership team have been working with the Martin Property Group on an MBO.

“While the Martin Property Group is their preferred partner, the leadership team’s sole intention is to work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that’s already taking shape.”

data.title: Bailey: Businesses are cutting costs to cope with Iran war energy shock
data.description:
Businesses hit by the Iran war are choosing to cut costs rather than pass on price rises to struggling households, Andrew Bailey has said.

The Governor of the Bank of England suggested inflation in Britain had been kept in check by bosses opting to squeeze profits to combat higher energy bills caused by the conflict.

However, he warned that companies would find this “harder” the longer the war in the Middle East dragged on.

Speaking at the Institute of International Finance’s annual meeting in Bangkok, Mr Bailey said: “Talking to businesses, there is a very, very big focus on cost cutting and a very big focus on the difficulty of passing through.

“Firms are clearly squeezing margins as well as cost cutting, using margins. The longer the energy situation goes on, the harder that gets.”

Mr Bailey also noted that soaring mortgage rates had kept inflation under control by reducing homeowners’ disposable income and limiting their ability to spend.

He added: “Our mortgage rates have gone up, they’re pretty much the top end of the G7, in terms of increases in mortgage rates.”

Mr Bailey’s comments suggest that he may be willing to wait longer to assess the impact of a prolonged conflict before considering an increase in interest rates.

However, investors are still pricing in a 93pc chance of an interest rate rise next month.

The Governor cautioned that it was “too early” to draw firm conclusions about the impact, with the Bank’s next interest rate decision published just days after John Healey’s maiden Budget on Oct 28.

But Mr Bailey insisted he was not complacent, noting that the economy had been more “resilient” to the oil price shock than initially expected.

The Bank kept interest rates on hold at 3.75pc in September, although three members of its Monetary Policy Committee voted for a rate rise to 4pc, including the Bank’s chief economist.

Mr Bailey said he had been surprised by how the economy had been able to weather the oil price shock, even as diesel prices hit £2 a litre.

The economy grew by 0.1pc in August, defying analysts’ expectations. However, Mr Bailey noted that growth remained weak by historical standards.

“It’s not as strong a growth as frankly we need. It’s not as strong a growth as we’ve had in the past. But there are signs,” said Mr Bailey.

He added that investment remained a source of support, while consumers were able to “smooth consumption” by dipping into what analysts have estimated is a £1tn savings reserve built up during the pandemic.

Figures from Moneyfacts show that the average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6pc for the first time in three years, adding hundreds of pounds to monthly payments for some borrowers.

The Bank previously said 1.3 million UK homeowners may face higher mortgage payments by the end of 2028 as a result of the war in the Middle East.

Kevin Warsh, the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, also said he was surprised at the resilience of the global economy.

“Almost everywhere in the global economy is showing resilience that I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what’s happening in geopolitics and hotspots around the world,” he said.

However, Mr Warsh said he would not “pre-judge” future decisions before the Federal Reserve’s next meeting later this month.

The central banker repeated that he was an optimist on AI but warned that the transition would be a “very bumpy one”.

Speaking on a separate panel in Bangkok, he said: “It’s going to change the real economy. We don’t know in the next 12 or 18 months its effect on employment [but] we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing.

“But the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one. Bumpy in our understanding of the technology. Bumpy because we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies.”

data.title: School coaches face the axe as diesel prices soar
data.description:
Thousands of school coach services are facing the axe as soaring diesel prices make it impossible for operators to turn a profit.

Almost half the coach firms that take 600,000 children to school each weekday plan to quit if fuel prices do not fall soon, according to the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT).

It would leave pupils in rural locations struggling to get to lessons and heap costs on local authorities, who have a duty to provide them with free transport if the nearest school is too far to walk.

Graham Vidler, the CPT’s chief executive, said school contracts were negotiated for the full academic year at fixed rates, leaving coach operators haemorrhaging cash after a jump of more than 40pc in diesel prices since the start of the Iran war.

Mr Vidler called on John Healey, the Chancellor, to grant school coaches a fuel duty rebate of 20p per litre of diesel in the Budget.

He said: “This industry operates on narrow margins and school work is generally done on a fixed-price basis – so if your costs go up, you have to take a loss or hand the contract back.

“Our members are on a knife edge. A quarter have already reduced operations, two thirds say they’re concerned about their viability and some operators have gone out of business.”

Coach operators that once relied on school contracts for steady income have come to regard them as a burden, the CPT said.

A survey last week of more than 500 members, which operate around 10,000 coaches, found that 45pc were planning to pull out of school services next year.

Mr Vidler warned this would have a “huge impact on local authorities, independent schools and people trying to get their children to school”.

He added that a 20p rebate from the Chancellor would reduce the cost of diesel for coach businesses by about 13pc. Coach operators can claim back the VAT on their diesel, paying about 160p a litre.

If coach companies pull out of school contracts, Mr Vidler said commitments under the Education Act could compel authorities to ferry children to school in taxis or fleets of minibuses.

Pupils under eight must be provided with free transport for journeys of more than two miles, rising to three miles for older children.

While the Government has provided a one-off payment of £30m to help mitigate soaring diesel prices, Mr Vidler said that had gone overwhelmingly to urban bus operators.

Coaches for tourist excursions, sporting events and rail replacement services are generally negotiated at shorter notice than school contracts, making them more sustainable for businesses, he said.

He said the industry nevertheless expected to see fewer trips in the coming months to attractions such as Christmas markets.

The situation is particularly acute because coach operators – which provide 450 million passenger journeys each year, equivalent to 25pc of the total for rail – are mostly family-owned and have more limited financial resources than major urban bus operators.

Operators have formed a new association, Coach UK, to help press their concerns with ministers.

data.title: Fashion labels favoured by Princess of Wales hit by cyber attack
data.description:
The parent company of fashion brands favoured by the Princess of Wales has apologised to customers after it was hit by a cyber attack.

The Foschini Group (TFG) London – the fashion group that includes Hobbs and Whistles, whose dresses and coats have often been worn by the Princess – told customers on Tuesday that it had suffered a “cyber security incident”.

The South African retail group said it became aware of the attack affecting its UK business on Sunday.

It said the hack had affected “certain of its IT systems” – specifically its Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles brands.

The company said there was no reason to believe customers’ payment information was at risk.

In an email to customers, the company said: “On Sunday 11th October, TFG London identified a cyber security incident affecting some of our IT systems.

“As soon as we identified the incident, we activated our business continuity plan, engaged external cyber security experts and informed relevant authorities. Our investigation is ongoing and we are working hard to get all our systems back up and running as quickly and safely as we can.

“All our stores are open as normal and our teams will be happy to welcome you.”

Orders made on or after Sunday may be delayed, the company warned, but it urged customers not to reorder.

TFG is the latest retailer to suffer a cyber attack, after Asos confirmed a potential data breach after hackers sent a smartphone alert to thousands of its customers.

Asos said last week that the hackers tricked an employee into sharing login details. The hackers gained access to some personal information, including names and contact details. However, it is thought that no payment card information or account passwords were accessed.

TFG first entered the UK market in 2015 by buying Phase Eight and has since added womenswear brands Whistles and Hobbs, homeware brand Inside Story and lifestyle brand White Stuff to its portfolio.

Headquartered in London, the group now employs 3,000 people. Inside Story and White Stuff have not been affected by the cyber attack.

In an email to customers, TFG said it did not believe any payment information had been stolen.

“Importantly, payment processing is carried out by a third-party provider,” the email said. “Based on our investigation so far, we have no reason to believe that payment information is at risk.

“As our investigation continues, we will be working to identify if any sensitive information related to our customers was impacted.

“If we determine that your personal information was affected, you will be directly informed. We do not believe it is necessary to change your account login information at this time.

“We know this news may be unsettling and we’re committed to keeping you updated as we have more information to share.”

data.title: BBC to ‘rest’ DIY SOS amid funding challenges
data.description:
The BBC has confirmed its long-running home-renovation TV series DIY SOS will be “rested” next year amid the corporation’s ongoing funding challenges.

The programme, hosted by Nick Knowles, helps transform the homes of families facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.

First aired in 1999, it began as a low-budget show in which Knowles and a small team helped homeowners fix botched DIY projects.

In 2010, the TV series relaunched as DIY SOS: The Big Build and shifted to larger-scale projects that saw the team repair and transform people’s homes across Britain with help from local communities.

The BBC has confirmed the show will be “rested” after its latest series currently on air, and replaced by a spin-off show revisiting past projects.

A BBC spokesman said: “In light of the BBC’s savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore.

“DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show’s past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year.”

The BBC has also confirmed its annual Children In Need instalment of DIY SOS, which involves a large-scale charitable build often focused on supporting vulnerable young people, has been rested.

The decisions come amid a series of recent cuts by the corporation as part of the first phase of its effort to save £500m in the next three years, which have included the cancellation of TV shows Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.

DIY SOS has taken on many ambitious projects through the years, including in 2015, Knowles worked with the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Sussex and hundreds of volunteers to transform a derelict street in Manchester into housing for veterans.

The Prince of Wales returned to the programme in 2018 for its two-part special focused on supporting the survivors and community affected by the Grenfell Tower fire, which killed 72 people.

The episodes also saw the DIY SOS team build a brand-new community centre and restore the Dale Youth Boxing Club, which was destroyed in a fire in June 2017.

The programme launched its 35th series earlier this month with an episode which saw Knowles break down in tears during a “physically and emotionally draining” house renovation.

The TV host’s team helped 16-year-old Dan, who has spent the last three years in hospital after life-saving surgery to remove a brain tumour that left him with complex disabilities.

DIY SOS is available on BBC iPlayer, with new episodes airing weekly on BBC One.

data.title: Healey plans £1bn Budget crackdown on online retailers
data.description:
Labour is planning a £1bn crackdown on online retailers to fund cuts to business rates for high-street shops, according to reports.

The chancellor will use his maiden Budget to announce that multibillion-pound online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay will be held liable for collecting tax owed by retailers selling goods on their sites.

The policy, first reported by The Times, is expected to raise up to £1bn for the Treasury by closing a loophole whereby mainly overseas sellers take advantage of lax enforcement to avoid VAT.

During the Makerfield by-election, Andy Burnham pledged to increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high-street shops would be exempt from the tax altogether, at a cost of around £880m.

He said at the time that he wanted to help family-owned businesses, which were the “heart and soul of this country”, and give them “the chance to thrive”.

A Treasury source told the newspaper that John Healey’s priority was to “protect local family businesses and the high streets we love”.

They added: “That means having the beauticians and white van drivers of our towns at the forefront of his mind as the Budget draws nearer.”

Concerns about foreign retailers evading VAT have grown in recent years, with MPs warning HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) in 2025 that the £5.5bn lost to businesses exploiting weaknesses in the system every year is probably just the “tip of the iceberg”.

The Public Accounts Committee, the group of MPs that scrutinises government spending, has accused HMRC of failing to take tax evasion seriously. Overseas sellers avoid VAT and undercut British businesses by setting up fake companies.

Tens of thousands of British shell companies have been set up by Chinese citizens in recent years, giving them VAT numbers they can use to register as UK sellers on online platforms.

Their accounts are then shut down before payment of VAT is demanded. There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the marketplaces in which they operate.

Under the new proposal, online marketplaces will be responsible for collecting VAT at the point of sale from all sellers who have a yearly turnover of more than £90,000, according to The Times.

Mr Healey is expected to raise taxes in his first Budget to plug a multibillion-pound black hole caused by the Iran war.

On Monday the Institute for Fiscal Studies said the Chancellor faced a £35bn bill to maintain existing spending policies and to boost defence funding to 3 per cent of GDP by 2030.

On Tuesday, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned Mr Healey against unfunded giveaways to ease cost-of-living pressures.

The IMF also downgraded its outlook for British growth and warned of further price rises and job losses.

While the fund did not issue a direct warning to Britain, it said an urgent need to bring down borrowing meant help with cost-of-living pressures should be used sparingly by all countries.

With the Budget looming on Oct 28, Mr Healey has ruled out increasing capital gains tax to the same level as income tax.

He had been considering equalising the two but will not, for fear it would make Britain less attractive to investors.

The Treasury could still opt for a smaller increase in capital gains tax, which is currently 24 per cent for higher-rate taxpayers on the profits of asset sales, compared with up to 45 per cent for income tax.

A Treasury spokesman told The Telegraph: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: UAE claims about Telegraph bid demolished by Ofcom
data.description:
Britain’s media regulator delivered an emphatic rejection of the United Arab Emirates’ attempted takeover of The Telegraph, it has finally been revealed.

As the Gulf autocracy faces criticism in the UK over financial misconduct at Manchester City, an investigation by Ofcom into the bid for this newspaper by its investment vehicle RedBird IMI has been published two-and-a-half years after it was handed to ministers.

Its damning conclusion was that despite assurances, the UAE would have had the ability and the incentive to influence The Telegraph and damage the accuracy of news and the free expression of opinion. The deal would have been against the public interest, Ofcom warned.

The findings are likely to fuel anger over the UAE’s sham contracts and misleading accounting at Manchester City. The club denies wrongdoing but is threatened with relegation from the Premier League over the scandal linked to its owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the vice-president of the UAE.

He was also behind the Telegraph bid. In finding that RedBird IMI’s proposed undertakings on the editorial independence of The Telegraph should not be relied upon, Ofcom cited evidence it received about his Manchester City takeover.

The regulator said that despite Sheikh Mansour’s claims that the acquisition was a personal commercial investment, “senior Emirati government officials and advisers were soon appointed to senior roles at the club”.

Pierre Andrews, a director at consultancy Public First and a former adviser to the Culture Secretary, said: “The publication of this report couldn’t come at a worse time for this Government as Andy Burnham’s links to the UAE during his time as Manchester Mayor are under the microscope.

“Two years ago, the Telegraph takeover captured the political and public imagination. Now, the Manchester City saga has the potential to create an equivalent headache for Labour.”

Ofcom pointed to “significant overlap” between the leadership of IMI, the UAE media company which majority-financed the bid, and the Gulf state’s leaders.

It warned this gave the bidder “clear political and broader commercial incentives” to interfere in The Telegraph’s editorial line in a way that risked harming free speech and the accurate presentation of news in the UK.

The report highlighted that while, like other national newspaper publishers, The Telegraph’s revenues have fallen over the last decade, its profit margins are among the highest in the industry.

The publication of the report drew an immediate and angry response from the UAE in the pages of The National, its state-owned newspaper, at which Ofcom received evidence of state censorship.

A spokesman for IMI said: “Ofcom was tasked with assessing a commercial media company. It failed to do so.

“Instead of judging the RedBird IMI bid for The Telegraph on the facts, Ofcom based its assessment on an arbitrary and biased set of assumptions, conflating the commercial interests of a private company with the conduct of a sovereign state.”

The National also reported criticism of the UK from Nick Candy, the Reform treasurer, who said it harmed Britain’s standing as a destination for global investment. Mr Candy is a property developer with significant interests in Abu Dhabi and Dubai.

However, Mr Candy’s comments were contradicted by Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesman, who told The Telegraph: “We don’t want foreign interference in our politics. Burnham seems to have fallen into the trap as the last government.

“Now we need answers about what conversations Burnham had with Manchester City’s owners and what he got out of them.”

Ofcom’s report cited evidence that there was “no clear dividing line between the public and private sector” in the UAE.

The investigation was ultimately overtaken by events in Parliament, where an outcry by MPs and peers triggered legislation to ban foreign states from investing in UK news organisations.

That allowed the Conservative government of the time and its Labour successor to delay publication of Ofcom’s specific concerns about the UAE, which took great offence that its ambitions towards The Telegraph were thwarted.

Ofcom’s findings on the UAE are likely to raise questions over the Hollywood mega-merger of Paramount and Warner, which was completed this month. The Gulf state, alongside its regional neighbours Qatar and Saudi Arabia, invested billions of dollars in the deal, again alongside its US private equity partner RedBird Capital.

Paramount offered assurances on the editorial independence of the news channel CNN comparable to those it offered on The Telegraph. Unlike the UK, American authorities ultimately accepted them and waved the deal through.

The US media giant has also insisted that while its Gulf backers will own close to 50pc of the combined company, they will not hold any voting shares.

But Ofcom’s report found that Abu Dhabi held sway over RedBird Capital regardless of the governance structure, owing to their wider commercial relationship.

It said: “In practice, this position need never become explicit, since RedBird Capital’s own commitment to the success of the joint venture risks incentivising it to anticipate, on an ongoing basis, what IMI may want.”

Sportswashing and censorship fears

Ofcom dismissed RedBird IMI’s claims that the UAE would merely hold a “passive” ownership stake in the “influential” Telegraph. The regulator also expressed doubts over the bidder’s insistence that the complex £600m loan deal it signed with the financially troubled Barclay family to secure The Telegraph was a purely commercial venture and not a bid for influence.

It said: “Based on the information we have, the commercial rationale for the loan, taking account of the collateral assets and the loan’s size and risk profile, is not clear, even having regard to any additional value from deal certainty.

“We consider that it would be inappropriate at this stage to conclude that the loan was motivated only by commercial factors.”

The regulator said there was a “material risk” that IMI would have greater influence in the joint venture than the formal ownership structure suggested, particularly given the make-up of its board.

IMI is chaired by Sultan Ahmed Al-Jaber, an Emirati politician who also leads Abu Dhabi’s state-owned oil company. Mr Jaber has also been accused of shaping the Gulf state’s censorship regime during his time as chairman of its media regulator, earning him the moniker of “censor-in-chief”.

Ofcom said: “We consider that these factors alone may give IMI the ability to exercise influence over editorial decisions by TMG so as to adversely impact the accuracy of news and free expression of opinion.”

The regulator cited particular concerns from respondents about the risk of “sportswashing” given Sheikh Mansour’s grip over football clubs in the UK and worldwide.

In addition to the UAE’s ability to exert active influence, Ofcom pointed to warnings about the risk of self-censorship by journalists and editors.

RedBird IMI attempted to draw comparisons between its Telegraph bid and undertakings made by Rupert Murdoch in 1981 to protect editorial independence at the Times and Sunday Times newspapers.

But Ofcom said there were “fundamental differences” between a newspaper being owned by a state compared to a powerful individual or corporation.

It said: “All else equal, a state or government owning, or holding a majority interest in, a newspaper would put it in a position to use its influence on that paper to further its foreign policy, commercial, reputational, or other ambitions.”

Ofcom, which received 35 responses to its consultation as well as a string of letters from MPs and peers, highlighted a “culture of restricting free expression” in the UAE.

It pointed to laws requiring all media outlets in the UAE to comply with restrictive “standards” and harsh punishments, including up to five years’ imprisonment, for anyone deemed to have sullied the state’s reputation.

Amnesty International has condemned the UAE’s laws, saying they “significantly curtail freedom of expression and assembly”.

The UAE ranked 158th out of 180 countries in the latest Reporters Without Borders World Press Freedom Index, having dropped steadily from a rank of 114 in 2013.

Ofcom cited previous breaches by the state-owned channel ADMC, which held a UK broadcasting licence until 2021.

The channel was twice found in breach of broadcasting rules over its coverage of the UAE and Qatar, with the regulator condemning its “comprehensive failure” and handing down a £125,000 fine.

Ofcom also pointed to allegations of interference by government officials in The National, an English-language daily newspaper also owned by IMI.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: Grid operator spends £50m in a single day to keep the lights on
data.description:
Britain’s grid operator is facing fresh questions about how it manages the electricity system after paying nearly £50m in a single day to keep the lights on.

National Energy System Operator (Neso) paid an estimated £49m in so-called “balancing costs” on Wednesday in what is thought to be a record.

It was the second day of record-breaking payments to keep the grid stable. Neso paid out £39.4m on Tuesday, according to provisional figures.

Some of the money went to Scottish wind farms to switch off because the grid was incapable of transmitting all their power. However, most of the money went to gas-fired power stations in England, which were paid to ramp up their output to replace the missing green power.

Data from leading energy consultancy LCP Delta showed that balancing costs hit a record £505m in September. The annual bill is set to grow from an estimated £2bn this year to £8bn by 2028. The costs are ultimately passed on to households and businesses in the form of higher bills.

Neso said it was legally obliged to make balancing payments and blamed the slow construction of new pylons and power lines for the rapid rise in costs.

A spokesman said: “The single biggest opportunity to reduce balancing costs is the timely delivery of new infrastructure by transmission owners, which could halve balancing costs by the end of the decade.”

The UK has three monopoly transmission networks. SSE and Scottish Power run networks in northern and southern Scotland, respectively, while National Grid owns the system in England and Wales.

However, Andrew Bowie, the Conservative shadow energy secretary, said Neso had to answer questions about rapidly rising costs.

“What is going on at Neso? Why are their models so wrong?” he wrote on X. He said the spending was “unsustainable”.

Other worrying incidents at Neso have occurred, including demand-forecasting errors, margin notices in which Neso pays generators up to five times the normal rate for extra power, and emergency requests to other European countries to supply more electricity.

The grid faced multiple warnings of frequency fluctuations on Thursday. It aims to keep the frequency of its alternating current between 49.8 and 50.2 hertz, but the system went both above and below these levels through the morning, although it remained within wider statutory limits.

The grid operator, taken into public ownership in 2024 by Ed Miliband, the then energy secretary at the time, is already facing scrutiny for how it managed the network during a summer incident.

Two reports on its handling of a June power-supply crisis that put the UK at risk of blackouts are due next week.

One commissioned by Neso will report on allegations that the organisation tried to cover up the incident. The other, overseen by regulator Ofgem, will examine the underlying technical failures.

An Ofgem spokesman said: “We are scrutinising Neso’s performance and pushing for every available measure to reduce constraint and balancing costs. Consumers should not pay a penny more than necessary.”

data.title: Seventy years ago, Britain led the way on nuclear power. Then we stopped
data.description:
In 1956, Calder Hall in Cumbria became the world’s first commercial-scale nuclear power station. Some of the world’s best scientists, and engineers came together to help build and deliver an industry that would become the envy of the world – right here in the UK. Then, gradually, we stopped.

Seventy years on, the UK is embarking on another major infrastructure programme with nuclear power at its heart. The question is, however, what would the country look like today had we kept building?

You only have to look across the Channel. March 6, 1974 is a date that arguably changed French energy history forever. That day, the country’s prime minister, Pierre Messmer, announced a programme to build nuclear power stations across France. And they built at scale. Today, approximately 70 per cent of France’s electricity comes from nuclear energy. In the UK, nuclear generates only around 12 per cent.

But the UK had a head start. Had we kept building, today we would see much cheaper, more secure electricity, less dependency on volatile international gas markets, and tens of thousands more people employed in highly skilled infrastructure jobs.

Instead, we allowed an industry that the UK pioneered to become one we have had to rebuild. I began my career at Dungeness nuclear power station as a craft electrical apprentice in 1980. I have spent decades working in this industry and have seen what it can deliver. I have also seen the consequences when projects become isolated, one-off undertakings.

When you stop building, experienced workers leave, supply chains disappear, and expertise is lost. When you eventually start again, you pay to rebuild much of it. That is an expensive way to run an industry. It is an even worse way to secure a country’s energy future and protect its energy security. That’s why we need to keep building.

The next generation of nuclear power stations must be treated as a programme, a fleet, not a series of disconnected projects.

Sizewell C has an advantage. We have taken the design developed for Hinkley Point C and using the experience gained there to build more efficiently. But that doesn’t mean we are building it exactly the same way.

The design is already established. That means we can focus on improving how we build – on more innovation. That means making greater use of off-site manufacturing, with large sections of the plant being assembled away from construction and brought in ready for installation. We are also making better use of digital technologies to plan construction and ensure components arrive on site when they are needed, as opposed to waiting to be installed.

But innovation can’t be stifled by too much regulation.

It is important to confront the regulatory and planning processes that have made major infrastructure unnecessarily difficult to deliver. The Fingleton review, commissioned by the Government to examine how nuclear regulation could be improved, identified a system that had become too complex. Its recommendations offer an opportunity to remove duplication, improve decision-making, and get projects moving more quickly.

This is a definite moment for the UK’s nuclear sector. A once-in-a-generation opportunity to strike a better balance between preserving the UK’s world-class safety, security and environmental standards while making nuclear delivery simpler, more proportionate and more predictable.

We have a simple formula. Keep the design consistent, learn from what has happened before, and get better at building it. The next project should be able to go even further.

And there is a bigger prize at stake here too. Sizewell C is expected to create tens of thousands of jobs and deliver 1500 apprenticeships. Seventy per cent of our construction value is expected to go to UK businesses. This is an opportunity for engineers, welders, electricians, and manufacturers, in addition to giving young people who are not in education, employment or training a route into skilled, well-paid work. But suppliers need confidence to invest in people, and that confidence will only come from knowing there will be another project after this one.

The case for nuclear is about far more than electricity generation – it’s about keeping the lights on when the wind isn’t blowing, protecting households and businesses from international energy shocks, and creating skilled, well-paid jobs that can sustain communities for generations. 

A ten-year-old child today could still be receiving electricity from Sizewell C long after they have retired. Which brings me to an old Greek proverb: “A society grows great when old men plant trees in whose shade they shall never sit.” Nuclear power requires precisely that kind of thinking.

The people making the decisions today may never see the full benefits of the infrastructure they approve. But their children and grandchildren will. Seventy years ago, the UK showed the world what nuclear power could achieve. Now, let’s build on what we’ve started.

Nigel Cann is chief executive of Sizewell C

data.title: Germany’s battle to break its economic addiction to China turns existential
data.description:
For decades, Germany seemed immune to the China shock that has wreaked havoc on Western manufacturers.

After Beijing joined the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 2001 and flooded markets with cheap goods, Germany’s carmakers and chemicals producers not only stood strong but benefited from selling to the new Chinese market.

However, German policymakers and industrialists became complacent as China pursued closer business ties. Cue what economists have coined the “China Shock 2.0” and Germany is suddenly one of the most vulnerable countries in the world.

Now, German-China relations are undergoing a sea change as Chancellor Friedrich Merz wakes up to how Beijing’s new era of global dominance is hammering the German economy.

As recently as 2020, Germany had a trade surplus of nearly €20bn (£17bn) with China. This is now a deficit of €21bn.

Analysis by the Global Public Policy Institute shows that while many countries, including the UK, have reduced their exposure to China in recent years, Germany has become increasingly vulnerable. Since 2013, Germany has moved from the 10th most exposed country to China to the third, behind only South Korea and Russia.

In a Centre for European Reform paper earlier this year, economists Sander Tordoir and Brad Setser warned that “China Shock 2.0” is similar in scale to the first one, which followed China’s accession to the WTO in 2001. Back then, China’s manufacturing surplus climbed to nearly 1pc of global GDP. In the last four years, this has grown by almost another percentage point.

But this time the shock is more existential. In the 2000s, when the West lost manufacturers who made toys, furniture and basic electronics, they did not lose sectors that were central to the future dynamism of their economies, Tordoir and Setser argued.

Countries such as Germany also gained major new export markets in chemicals and machinery. This time, China is not increasing its imports. And the sectors that it is now competing with – namely cars, machinery and chemicals – are vitally important to Germany’s economy.

Chinese goods are now not only cheap but high quality and Germany is suddenly seeing its core exports squeezed out of China and other foreign markets, but also at home.

“For years, the German elites told themselves that interdependence meant mutual dependence, but the latest numbers look less comfortable,” says Sari Arho Havrén, a China foreign-relations specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).

Cars, an industry which Germany has dominated for decades, are at the heart of this second wave of Chinese exports.

Analysts had expected that China would export 10 million cars a year by the end of the decade. But on an annualised basis, China’s car exports hit this threshold in the last three months of 2025.

“In the automobile sector, the tipping point was really when Chinese companies started leading the field in electric vehicles and hybrid cars,” says Jessie Yin, associate director at the Atlantic Council’s Geoeconomics Centre.

This is one reason why China’s export volumes last year grew at more than double the pace of global trade.

As China’s star ascends, Germany is left flailing. Its exports have been falling steadily since 2018 and dropped by around 5pc last year. The industries most exposed to Chinese competition have been shrinking most markedly. Its industrial production has been falling for six years and economic output is still around 6pc below its pre-pandemic trajectory.

Tordoir and Setser, of the Centre for European Reform, warn: “China shock is now the most important cause of Germany’s malaise.”

It has much further to fall. A report published earlier this year by the French prime minister’s planning office warned Chinese competition could threaten 70pc of Germany’s manufacturing output over the medium term.

Merz is now trying to claw back control.

On his first visit as chancellor to Beijing in February, Merz warned that Germany’s trade deficit with China had quadrupled in five years, diagnosing it as “not healthy”. He has warned several times of signs that China is manipulating its currency.

This month, in a joint letter with Emmanuel Macron, the French president, he called on Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to bring in a mechanism to allow the EU to impose faster restrictions on countries engaging in harmful trade practices.

And just last week, Germany blocked Chinese state-owned shipping company Cosco from purchasing a logistics group in Germany’s largest seaport.

The politics are only just shifting, because China has pursued a trade and investment strategy that means many German companies have become hooked on Beijing for growth.

Havrén, of Rusi, says China has developed close business ties with Germany and made a swathe of investments in infrastructure projects to gain political influence.

“China works quite a lot through German businesses,” she says.

“These big companies want to maintain relations and they have powerful lobbies that flow through to the German governments. China wants to keep Germany as the brake in Brussels. If Berlin hesitates, the EU hesitates.

“Part of German business still see China as indispensable if they want to scale.” German firms increased investment by roughly a third in the first half of this year, Havrén adds.

China also holds control over the world’s supply of rare earth minerals, which are vital for German manufacturers. When China weaponised this supply chain in a standoff with the US last year, Germany’s car industry was brought almost to a halt.

“The dependencies run so deep that China gains a lot of political leverage through these actions,” adds Havrén.

German businesses are now turning against China. In August, the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry called on Merz for a tougher stance on China.

But policymakers have made little headway. China flatly rejected European requests to commit to some form of export restraint, particularly for hybrid cars, at EU-China trade talks last week. The European Commission is discussing “safeguard” trade defence measures, prompting fear of escalation.

“I think China would likely retaliate in one way or another. There is a big risk of a trade war,” says Havrén.

“But China has so much leverage. I’m not sure the EU can afford that.”

data.title: Lisa Nandy ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s £1.6bn ITV takeover
data.description:
Lisa Nandy is preparing to intervene in Sky’s £1.6bn takeover of ITV owing to concerns about media plurality and freedom of speech.

The Culture Secretary said she was “minded to” intervene in the merger, which will see US-owned Sky take control of ITV’s channels and streaming service.

As well as focusing on freedom of expression and plurality of views in news media, Ms Nandy’s potential intervention relates to the need to avoid concentration of media ownership across the UK.

The Culture Secretary cited public interest concerns over the effect of the deal on streaming.

Current legislation only allows ministers to intervene in deals concerning broadcast television, although Ms Nandy said she was considering expanding it to cover on-demand programmes.

Sky and ITV have until Oct 20 to respond, after which Ms Nandy will decide whether to issue a public interest intervention notice.

This would trigger investigations by both Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority into the effect of the deal.

Dame Carolyn McCall, ITV’s chief executive, has previously said she expected the deal to undergo an in-depth review lasting up to 18 months.

Sky’s swoop on ITV comes amid a broader reshaping of the media landscape as traditional broadcasters seek scale to compete with deep-pocketed US rivals.

If approved, the deal will bring together Sky’s subscription TV business with the broadcaster behind shows including I’m A Celebrity Get Me Out of Here and Love Island.

The deal does not include ITV’s lucrative production business, which will remain a standalone company on the London Stock Exchange.

The merger has already attracted political scrutiny as it will hand control of ITV’s channels to Comcast, the US media conglomerate behind Sky.

While bosses have pledged to keep ITV News and Sky News separate until at least 2031, the merger has also prompted concerns about news provision in the UK, especially in regional news.

Channel 4 is also expected to raise concerns about the effect of the tie-up on the advertising market, given the combined company would hold significant market power.

Ms Nandy’s involvement in the deal came just months after she threatened to intervene in Paramount’s $110bn (£83bn) takeover of Warner Bros.

However, she ultimately waved the deal through after Paramount, which owns Channel 5 in the UK, pledged to increase investment in British programming.

An ITV spokesman said: “We welcome the publication of the Secretary of State’s ‘minded to’ issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully cooperating in the process.

“This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries.”

A Sky spokesman said: “We will carefully consider the Secretary of State’s letter and look forward to engaging constructively as the review progresses.

“We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV’s Media and Entertainment business together will create a stronger British media business, better able to compete with global streaming platforms, support great British programming and trusted news, and deliver more for audiences.

“We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV’s identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices.”
