data.title: The rise and fall of British helicopters
data.description:
Do you have a favourite helicopter? Mine, as a child, was Airwolf. But it could have been the helicopter that dropped Anneka Rice off at so many castles in the pioneering 1980s Channel 4 game-show Treasure Hunt, or the Blue Thunder choppers that ferry our elite SAS teams around Britain, tackling emergencies.

Today, in addition to their use by armed forces, they are status symbols for the 0.01 per cent. Donald Trump used to owned a fleet of three Sikorsky S-76 helicopters, with predictably gilded interiors. Yet not so long ago, some believed this form of transport would be used regularly by the hoi polloi; hopping into a chopper would be as common as hailing a black cab.

This month marks 40 years since the demise of British Airways Helicopters, and that brief moment in time when it seemed scheduled passenger helicopter services might actually catch on. So why did the helicopter never go truly mainstream?

Up in the Airlink

Focke-Wulf’s FW61 was unveiled in the 1930s, before Russian-American pioneer Igor Sikorsky took up the baton in the 1940s. The US company he founded would go on to dominate these machines’ development for half a century.

But passenger helicopter services actually began in the UK. The route? From Liverpool to Cardiff, launched by BEA in 1950, with an intriguing stop in Wrexham that would have suited Rob McElhenney and Ryan Reynolds if it were operating today.

More BEA routes followed, such as Birmingham to Northolt, and on to Heathrow. Birmingham got a pioneering “Rotorstation” for helicopters to land at. It was opened at Heybarnes Recreation Ground in Hay Mills – Peaky Blinders territory. Three flights left for London daily.

Between 1978 and 1986, a helicopter shuttle service, dubbed the Airlink, connected Gatwick and Heathrow. This was before the M25 was finished and when the journey between the two main London airports was tortuous. Helicopters ferried transit passengers from apron to apron in minutes.

A vision of the future

The thinking among many was that helicopters would be omnipresent. During the Festival of Britain, there was a helicopter landing pad on the Southbank in London. The Southbank was earmarked for a more permanent heliport, which explains the brutalist design of the Queen Elizabeth Hall. It was supposed to protect against the noise and vibrations of helicopters.

In the end a heliport at Battersea was opened, further along the River Thames, and is still in use today. Architects’ designs for Sixties new towns always showed two things: a monorail, and helicopters fluttering in the sky. This was the vision of the future – back when we believed in a future that would be better.

Even the GPO became enamoured with helicopters and trialled their use to deliver post to the rural towns of Norfolk. Quite what Farmer Giles, drinking a pint of warm Bullard’s outside The Railway Inn in Docking on a Sunday afternoon in 1948, would have made of the sight of a GPO Sikorsky S-51 on a post run to Wells-Next-The-Sea is anyone’s guess.

In the Fifties, Britain ramped up its own helicopter production at Westland’s Yeovil site, which became the home of the British helicopter. The Dragonfly, Widgeon, Whirlwind and Wessex became instantly recognisable machines built in Somerset. The Sea King, Wasp and Scout followed, then it was into the era of more modern machines like the Puma, Gazelle and Lynx.

Away with the Faireys

Among the more bizarre ideas was the Fairey Rotodyne: a hybrid between a plane and a helicopter that doesn’t look a million miles away from the stretched fuselage of the Chinook. In 1959 it flew from Heathrow to Paris via Dover and Brussels, but it wouldn’t catch on. One of the problems was the immense noise its rotors generated. This was going to be a problem when it was clattering over the roofs of densely populated areas of South London on the way to Battersea Heliport.

Westland took over Fairey in the 1960s, but domestic helicopter production was to become a hot political potato. Britain’s varied and incredibly successful aerospace entities were walking a tightrope between innovating, investing, exporting and balancing the books. Their designs were legendary, but of course not everything worked. There was always a tussle between nationalising everything into what would become British Aerospace and selling parts off to foreign investors.

Westland became a political football during the so-called Westland Affair in 1985, which pitted different factions of Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative government against each other, as arguments raged over whether to maintain this facility in Yeovil, who should run it and who would pay for it.

End of an era

Why did helicopters fade away? As with other futuristic transport ideas like hovertrains, monorails, hovercraft and other “gadgetbahns”, their relatively high cost and niggling technical problems could never be fully resolved.

Aeroplanes, trains and cars driving on motorways won the transport arms race because they could be easily scaled, and eventually mass uptake drastically reduced costs. These forms of transport made money rather than costing it.

Motorways connect us. With the M40 complete, there was no need to take a helicopter from Birmingham to London. Helicopters are also gas guzzlers – even Porsche owners would baulk at the price of a full tank. Sabena wanted to follow the Rotodyne’s first international flight and start a helicopter from London to Brussels – but Eurostar does that journey more efficiently.

In the US, where traffic is terrible and public transport is worse, Blade has put up a fight, offering relatively affordable flights from JFK to Manhattan, but without the drama of the former Pan Am helicopter, which whisked passengers to the top of the Pan Am HQ in Midtown in the 1960s.

Helicopters are still popular as niche forms of transport, and incredibly useful for medical evacuations, police and military use, and VIP transport. UK Air Sea Rescue has used helicopters to rescue the lives of countless sailors around our shores, and helicopters have ferried thousands of workers to oil and gas rigs in the North Sea and beyond, from Aberdeen, Norwich, Humberside and other hubs.

But their mass-market use has dwindled in the face of competition – which is sad, because they have a real value. The experience of being in one is not like regular flying because you’re so low you can see everything below you. The feeling of rising into the sky for the first time is surreal.

Rare survivors

The Scilly Isles are one of the rare examples of a route where helicopters make sense, and these flights have continued on and off from 1964 to this day. My honeymooning parents cannot have been the only holidaymakers caught out by rough seas who needed to use the helicopter as a way to swiftly get off the islands. For locals, they are a lifeline back to the shops, schools and health services of Penzance. This is now the last surviving scheduled British helicopter service.

Nice to Monaco and Saint-Tropez are other popular services going strong, as are Helity’s routes from Malaga and Algeciras to the headline-grabbing Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Hong Kong to Macau is another example. Faroese flag carrier Atlantic Airways runs domestic helicopter flights. But anyone who’s gone puffin-spotting in Mykines, and found themselves stuck on the island for days due to bad weather, will know that helicopters aren’t much use in storms or low visibility, which is pretty much every day in a Faroe Islands winter.

For the super-rich class there will always be helicopters ready to take them to the British Grand Prix or Goodwood (two of the biggest weekends for the Battersea Heliport). But for the rest of us, the dream of flying everywhere by helicopter is elusive. It’s not impossible though – this is why helicopter aficionados specifically head to Tresco or Tórshavn.

data.title: All aboard! Princess of Wales escorts elderly to lunch on minibus
data.description:
The Princess of Wales jumped aboard a community minibus to take elderly people who live alone to a village lunch club.

The Princess, who has spoken regularly about the importance of community, went door-to-door with volunteers from the West Sussex Minibus service.

Her first stop of the morning was the tidy bungalow of Stella Drewett, 94, a former school cook.

Mrs Drewett was told of her VIP guest shortly beforehand and said: “I couldn’t quite believe it. I am quite a new member.

“It’s a great service. I used to drive myself until I decided to spare the other road users. Everyone said to me: ‘But what are you going to do now?’

“But they take me to the supermarket once a week and we go down to the village hall for the lunch club. It’s a very valuable service. It’s wonderful.”

The Princess put a reassuring hand on Mrs Drewett’s arm as she manoeuvred her walking frame along the garden path and told her: “Well done.”

She then stood behind Mrs Drewett as she climbed on board the minibus, putting her hands against her back as a precaution.

When the Princess asked about her trips out for lunch, the 94-year-old quipped that they meant “one day of not cooking”.

The Princess took a seat next to Mrs Drewett and joked about always forgetting her handbag.

“Everyone always runs after me [shouting] ‘you forgot your handbag’,” she said.

Encouraging her to put her seatbelt on, the Princess added: “I have to remind my children to put their seatbelts on too.”

All the passengers, including the Princess, were taken to Pulborough village hall for lunch and other activities.

Inside the hall, the Princess sat down at a table with Lynda Jones, 75, and discussed the washing up.

“I love washing up. I really do,” she said.

“Oh good, a volunteer!” joked another guest.

Asked whether her husband, the Prince of Wales, helped, the Princess said: “He does the drying. We are a good double act. And we get the children involved.”

Examining the food on the table, the Princess noted there was a bowl of crisps.

“I bet you never eat crisps,” Mrs Jones teased her.

“I do. I love salted,” the Princess replied, eating one as they spoke.

Sarah Broadhurst, 87, stopped by to thank the Princess for coming to Pulborough and they held hands as they chatted.

“I think it’s amazing she has come to our little place. It can be isolating so it is lovely to have a royal visit,” she said.

Outside the village hall, a small crowd had gathered after word spread about the visit, which had been kept secret.

The Princess also stopped to speak to Thea Botley, 25, with her sons Albie, 1, and Arthur, 3.

Albie held the Princess’s hand to jump off the curb.

“Look at your cool boots!” the Princess told him. “Jump? Well done. One more? Well done.”

“Sorry I’ve started something,” she laughed as Albie continued to jump as she walked off.

The Princess also said hello to Beatrix, 3, and stroked the ears of three-year old cocker spaniel Jack, as she chatted.

The Princess, who has two cocker spaniels herself, asked her: “Is he cheeky? Does he steal your food? Whenever there is cereal on the floor our doggies always eat the cereal!”

The day out was part of the Princess’s commitment to encourage real-life connection.

West Sussex Minibus is a member of the Community Transport Association, described by Kensington Palace as a “vital lifeline for people who cannot easily access public transport due to isolation, mobility challenges or financial barriers”.

The minibus service boarded by the Princess on Wednesday celebrates 50 years of service this year. It’s an all-volunteer community transport organisation supporting people living in rural West Sussex.

Established in response to the decline of rural public transport, the organisation has grown from a single volunteer-led minibus into a community transport network operating from eight village hubs, supported by 284 volunteers and a fleet of 11 minibuses.

Its fleet travels approximately 60,000 miles each year, providing around 13,000 passenger journeys.

data.title: Job fears as ‘vulture’ funds circle struggling rail-freight giant
data.description:
A struggling rail-freight business is being circled by dozens of private investment funds, stoking fears that it could be broken up.

DB Cargo UK, which operates more than 200 locomotives, has been put up for sale by Deutsche Bahn, its German owner, attracting interest from more than 40 potential bidders and investors.

However, unions fear that the business is unlikely to be sold to a single buyer and could be carved up, putting 2,300 jobs in doubt.

An industry source said it was “likely the bids will be from vulture capitalists”.

Aslef, which represents the firm’s 650 train drivers, said management had disclosed the interest from private funds in a document provided to staff.

The union said in its October newsletter that the document posed the question: “What happens if a buyer cannot be found?”

The company answered that it was “too early to speculate but we are currently talking to more than 40 debt and equity providers”.

James Glew, an Aslef official at DB Cargo, said: “The problem with this, from our point of view, is who they may sell the company to and what their intentions may or may not be.

“Everyone hopes the company will be acquired by someone who wants to run it as a going concern. But what for the future if it is acquired by an asset-stripping company?”

A source close to the sales process said a number of bids had also been received for the group as a whole.

The break-up fears have been compounded by DB Cargo UK’s poor financial performance in recent years.

The business owns dozens of potentially valuable brownfield sites across Britain, including 150 depots, terminals and railheads. Many are on the edges of urban areas and ripe for housing development.

Aslef said there were also concerns that DB Cargo’s fleet of 228 locomotives and 6,500 wagons could be sold abroad or even for scrap.

Simon Weller, Aslef’s assistant general secretary, claimed at the Trades Union Congress conference last month that Deutsche Bahn appeared intent on a “fire sale” of the UK business.

He said: “There is a lot of land up for sale. There is a huge amount of money in this sale in redevelopment.”

The Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association, which represents technical and office staff and managers at DB Cargo, said Deutsche Bahn had failed to rule out compulsory redundancies.

The Government has previously said it plans to expand the rail-freight sector 75pc by 2050 as it seeks to shift more cargo from road to rail.

DB Cargo was the dominant player in the rail-freight sector at the time of its privatisation in 1995, when it was known as English, Welsh & Scottish Railway, with a 90pc market share.

Deutsche Bahn bought the business for £309m in 2007. However, Britain’s industrial decline and the decision to close coal-fired power stations led to a slump in cargo volumes.

The UK arm had a £12m loss in 2024, down from £68m in 2023. Its market share dropped to 22pc in the three months through June, the lowest since records began, behind GB Railfreight and Freightliner.

A spokesman for Deutsche Bahn said the divestment process for DB Cargo UK was ongoing and that it could not comment further.

Interpath, which is advising on the auction, also declined to comment.

data.title: Mike Ashley tightens grip on Burberry
data.description:
Mike Ashley has tightened his grip on Burberry after upping his stake in the luxury brand, putting him on course to become the group’s biggest shareholder.

The billionaire’s Frasers Group now owns 7.4pc of the trench-coat maker, up from 6.3pc a fortnight ago, after using financial derivatives to add to his holding.

Frasers would become Burberry’s largest investor if Mr Ashley converts the derivatives to shares, a move which would give the fashion tycoon immense power over the 170-year-old fashion brand.

Burberry is worth more than £3.8bn, giving Frasers’ stake a value of about £280m. Mr Ashley’s group originally acquired a 4.2pc stake in the company during the summer.

The fashion house has struggled after an ill-timed push upmarket coincided with a global slowdown in luxury spending.

It reported a £66m loss last year and announced plans to cut 1,700 jobs, although there have been signs of a recovery under Joshua Schulman, its new chief executive.

Sales returned to growth in the three months to June, helped by renewed demand for its signature trench coats.

Burberry is the latest investment for Frasers, which owns Sports Direct and Flannels, after it spent months snapping up stakes in some of the industry’s biggest names.

Last week it unveiled an 8.8pc interest in American sportswear giant Under Armour, a major supplier to Sports Direct.

In August, it bought Harvey Nichols out of administration and has been locked in a bitter battle with the board of German fashion giant Hugo Boss over a potential takeover.

Frasers has amassed an interest of almost 50pc in the brand despite resistance from its leadership. The company also owns around 37pc of Mulberry, the British luxury handbag maker.

Its growing empire is part of a push by Michael Murray, Frasers’ chief executive and Mr Ashley’s son-in-law, to transform the business from a discount sportswear retailer into a major force in luxury fashion.

Last week, Frasers outlined plans to expand its Flannels department store chain across Europe and take the Harvey Nichols brand overseas.

Taking control of Burberry would give Mr Ashley ownership of one of Britain’s most recognisable fashion brands.

Mr Ashley has a history of taking minority stakes in retailers before seeking greater influence over their operations.

Frasers has also built positions in Asos and Boohoo,

However, its investments have not always paid off. Frasers bought luxury retailer Matches in late 2023 but placed it into administration less than three months later.

Burberry declined to comment. Frasers was approached for comment.

data.title: Octopus staff blocked from selling shares in employee fund
data.description:
Octopus employees have been blocked from selling shares in an employee equity scheme.

The investment firm has suspended a planned share sale after it was unable to meet a flood of withdrawal requests.

It marks the latest sign of turmoil at Octopus, which has been battling poor performance at one of its main funds, the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS).

Nearly 2,000 employees past and present were sent an email by bosses this week informing them of the decision.

The block will apply to a share scheme that is popular with its employees, allowing them to invest up to £150 a month from their gross salary into Octopus Group.

In return, they are granted 1.5 extra shares in the company for free.

As part of the scheme, Octopus runs an internal market where current staff and existing shareholders can buy and sell shares at a liquidity event each year.

However, the firm has now delayed the offer after the share sale was significantly oversubscribed and they were not able to meet the extent of withdrawals.

It comes after Octopus recently offered to waive its annual management charge for both existing and new investors in OITS, missing out on annual fees of around £100m.

The fund had been frozen for nearly three months, coinciding with a failed plan to acquire PlatformX Communications, the wholesale arm of TalkTalk.

However, after the deal collapsed two weeks ago, Octopus Investments said it would split the fund in two.

This led to Octopus permanently gating most of its fibre assets in the fund, which it has acknowledged as the biggest drag on performance.

Octopus said that the rest of the fund, which accounts for just over two thirds of its value, would be reopened. However, it warned that withdrawals could not be guaranteed.

OITS has 18,000 customers and allows investors to lower their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief.

Customers of OITS were sold shares in Fern Trading, which owns about 300 energy, property and telecoms companies.

The fund has come under growing scrutiny after The Telegraph revealed that savers had been bankrolling failed hospitals and care homes.

Investors in other Octopus funds have also struggled to get their money back.

Octopus blocked one financial adviser from withdrawing millions of pounds on behalf of his client from one of its schemes for seven months.

Mark Spendlove, of IPP Group, asked Octopus Investments – which manages inheritance tax funds – to withdraw £5.4m from Terido, a scheme aimed at small businesses.

The scheme takes the spare cash from member businesses and invests it in asset-backed loans, mainly in property, ensuring that its investors can qualify for business relief.

Octopus had told Mr Spendlove that the withdrawal process would take about four weeks, but later said that the money would be paid out over seven months, with the final £2m payment not made until March 2027.

OITS has also come under scrutiny for how it has been valuing its assets, particularly after it acknowledged the troubles in its fibre division.

It had previously committed to revaluing the holdings after the acquisition. However, they may not be revalued now until July 2027.

A spokesman for Octopus said: “We’ve always wanted as much of Octopus as possible to be owned by the people who work here, and we’re proud to have created a scheme that gives our employees the opportunity to become shareholders in the business.

“As part of that, since 2013 we’ve held an annual liquidity event which provides a mechanism for shareholders to buy and sell shares in Octopus. It is important to be clear that we haven’t cancelled this year’s event, it is simply delayed until later in the tax year.”

OITS has 18,000 customers and allows investors to lower their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief.

Customers of OITS were sold shares in Fern Trading, which owns about 300 energy, property and telecoms companies.

The fund has come under growing scrutiny after The Telegraph revealed that savers had been bankrolling failed hospitals and care homes.

Investors in other Octopus funds have also struggled to get their money back.

Octopus blocked one financial adviser from withdrawing millions of pounds on behalf of his client from one of its schemes for seven months.

Mark Spendlove, of IPP Group, asked Octopus Investments – which manages inheritance tax funds – to withdraw £5.4m from Terido, a scheme aimed at small businesses.

The scheme takes the spare cash from member businesses and invests it in asset-backed loans, mainly in property, ensuring that its investors can qualify for business relief.

Octopus had told Mr Spendlove that the withdrawal process would take about four weeks, but later said that the money would be paid out over seven months, with the final £2m payment not made until March 2027.

OITS has also come under scrutiny for how it has been valuing its assets, particularly after it acknowledged the troubles in its fibre division.

It had previously committed to revaluing the holdings after the acquisition. However, they may not be revalued now until July 2027.

A spokesman for Octopus said: “We’ve always wanted as much of Octopus as possible to be owned by the people who work here, and we’re proud to have created a scheme that gives our employees the opportunity to become shareholders in the business.

“As part of that, since 2013 we’ve held an annual liquidity event which provides a mechanism for shareholders to buy and sell shares in Octopus. It is important to be clear that we haven’t cancelled this year’s event, it is simply delayed until later in the tax year.”

data.title: US inflation jumps ahead of crunch midterm elections
data.description:
US inflation rose more than expected last month as diesel prices hit record highs just weeks before key mid-term elections to decide who controls Congress.

The consumer prices index rose from 3.4pc in August to 3.7pc in September, the US Department of Labor said, outstripping estimates of a jump to 3.6pc.

More than half of the increase in inflation last month was as a result of surging fuel prices, which climbed by 9.1pc during September.

The higher-than-expected figure sent the cost of US government borrowing surging on Wednesday as traders ramped up bets on the Federal Reserve (Fed) raising interest rates to temper price rises.

The data were published after the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that the global diesel crisis will drag on into next year despite Donald Trump’s claims to have unlocked crucial extra supplies.

The Paris-based organisation said diesel supplies “remained under significant strain” as exports from Russia and the Middle East were disrupted by conflict.

Diesel shortages are expected to continue well into next year, even as record prices are forecast to cause a decline in demand.

In its monthly oil market report, the IEA said: “Despite lower demand, oil market balances are forecast to remain in deficit through the end of the year, with constrained middle distillate supplies likely to persist well into 2027.”

Middle distillate refers to products such as diesel and jet fuel that are created during the refining process.

The IEA’s warning and the jump in inflation are a setback to Mr Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices for motorists before the US midterm elections on Nov 3.

The elections will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats control Congress.

The G7 announced the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel stockpiles earlier this month after pressure from the US president.

Mr Trump had threatened to impose an export ban on diesel as shortages pushed up the price of gasoline in the US to a record above $6.50 a gallon.

He also lifted sanctions on Russian diesel during the weekend in an effort to boost supplies, a move that drew criticism from the international community and members of his own Republican Party.

Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister, described Mr Trump’s agreement on Russian diesel as a “very risky” decision.

She warned on Wednesday that the agreement could send “contradictory” signals at a time when Western countries, including the US, have been seeking to pressure Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine, which has raged since Russia’s invasion in 2022.

The US president has blamed Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries for the increase in diesel prices.

While this has stretched global supplies, analysts say that Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and Mr Trump’s attack on Iran have also contributed to spiralling energy costs.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4pc after the latest inflation figures and was on track for a fifth loss in the six days since setting its record high.

Stocks were under pressure from rising borrowing costs, as expectations of higher US interest rates pushed the two-year US Treasury bond yield from 4.79pc to as high as 4.95pc.

Traders are betting that there is around a 47pc chance that the Fed will raise rates to combat rising inflation, compared to odds of 23pc on Tuesday.

Inflation pressures show little sign of easing. The IEA said global oil stocks declined in September after 113 million barrels were drawn down from inventories.

Global diesel exports fell by 700,000 barrels per day in September compared to the same month last year.

The Paris-based organisation said continued disruptions to Middle East exports, compounded by lower supply from Russia and some Asian countries, had cut global diesel availability. This was “putting diesel markets under extreme pressure”.

Diesel remains around £2 a litre at the pumps in the UK, according to RAC, having hit a record high last month.

John Healey, the Chancellor, is under pressure to scrap a planned 5p increase in fuel duty when he delivers his first Budget on Oct 28.

The IEA said high prices were taking their toll on global oil demand, which is expected to drop by 2.5 million barrels per day in the final three months of the year.

Oil was trading at around $106 a barrel on Wednesday, up from around $70 before the start of the Iran war.

Prices showed no sign of easing after a series of strikes on Saudi airports by Houthi rebels. The headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco was also hit during a missile attack on Wednesday.

data.title: If Amol Rajan wants to be the next Tucker Carlson, he needs people to actually watch him
data.description:
For the first interviewee on his new YouTube channel, Amol Rajan could have done much worse than Sir Gareth Southgate. The former England manager is a household name, widely admired, who has not given many recent interviews. Rajan was fresh off the back of an (admittedly curtailed) appearance on the much-watched Celebrity Traitors. Blockbuster stuff, at least on the team sheet.

But at the time of writing, their two-hour recording had accumulated 3,000 views and 85 likes, including those who watched the interview when it was broadcast live Thursday morning (during the first few minutes the number of viewers was in the 40s). Forget Wembley: their audience might have struggled to fill Truro City. Rajan is dreaming big, but on the evidence of the debut it might be harder going than he envisaged.

There was a time when journalists, tradesmen that they are, could dream of only a handful of career peaks. You might become an editor or a famous columnist, write a bestseller, get yourself on the telly or make a lucrative sideways move into PR. That was about it.

Barely into his 40s, Amol Rajan has already achieved several of these goals. He edited The Independent at a prodigiously young age. When he was a presenter on the Today programme, nearly six million people heard him grill politicians at breakfast time. Succeeding Jeremy Paxman as host of University Challenge, Rajan has been burnished by proximity to some of the nation’s nerdiest young people.

He was the lovable South London charmer, a state-school boy in a sea of private education, well on his way to national treasure status. According to published figures, he was paid more than £300,000 annually for his BBC work and earned more than £100,000 in outside gigs. A good life, by most measures.

But being a famous journalist is not enough these days. One must become a media empire.

“The BBC, and BBC News, is going to get smaller at an accelerating rate. And I want to go to where the action is,” Rajan has explained (on George Osborne’s podcast).

The internet’s enormous scale has allowed humble hacks to dream of industrial wealth. Hence the Amol Rajan Connection website, a “great digital Narnia” that promises to be a home for Rajan’s YouTube channel, newsletters, events and other content to help his audience navigate a big, scary world. While Rajan has yet to divulge all the details of the content, there are already a number of options to pay, including a “Negroni” tier (£299 a year, which includes a “virtual meet & greet with Amol”) and a “Pina Colada” (£999 for life membership, featuring a “meet & greet at all live events you attend”). Presumably at some stage there will be T-shirts. Thursday’s broadcast was, according to the blurb on YouTube, “brought to you in partnership with” an impressive array of sponsors, including Amazon, NatWest and Waitrose.

To an extent we can blame Gary Lineker for this curious state of affairs. The former England striker’s unlikely reinvention as an audiovisual tycoon with Goalhanger, responsible for the Rest Is… stable of podcasts, has pound signs spinning all over Fleet Street. Then there are Tucker Carlson and Piers Morgan, who have set up their own channels with great success. Carlson has nearly six millions subscribers on YouTube; Morgan is not far behind on 4.5 million. They have proved it is possible to build a large audience while cutting out the pesky networks.

But both men have finely tuned instincts for outrage, not to mention an appetite for confrontation. Carlson was forged in the reactionary fires of Fox News, Morgan in Nineties tabloids. They know that the internet loves rage, have no qualms about encouraging it and have hired smart people to maximise its impact. Rajan’s interview with Southgate – covering the not-unfamiliar territory of the former England manager’s career and concerns about problems facing young men – was perfectly fluent and thoughtful, but on the Today programme he would have been expected to generate multiple headlines.

It will not stop him, or others, from trying their luck. He is not alone in being lured away from his parent institution by the promise of online megastardom. Marina Hyde, the longtime Guardian columnist, recently quit to focus on podcasts, having developed a taste for it alongside Richard Osman on Lineker’s The Rest Is Entertainment. Holly Willoughby, the TV presenter, recently started her own YouTube channel, in which she chunters amiably with other celebrities. She has had disappointing viewing figures, too. Her channel is called Holly Willoughby Together. “Together” and “Connection”. They are positive, hopeful ideas. But positivity and hope do not do well online.

data.title: Healey must not launch another tax raid on banks
data.description:
It has been rare since the financial crash to hear a chancellor single out Britain’s banks for praise. So it was welcome that John Healey on Thursday described them as part of the “jewel in the British economic crown”. Having taken this enlightened stance, however, is he really going to use his Budget to launch yet another tax raid on one of Britain’s most productive sectors?

Reports indicate that this is one of the options the Chancellor is now considering, as he seeks to shore up the public finances. Unions are angry that banks are back to making healthy profits, after the lean years following the financial crisis. They are calling on Mr Healey to increase the surcharge that banks pay on top of ordinary corporation tax.

That might appease Leftists who do not understand why a profitable banking sector is vital to a healthy economy. Banks are one of Britain’s few remaining sources of high-value employment, their lending supports households and businesses, and financial services are a significant export earner for the country.

A tax rise would be hugely damaging not just to the banks, but to the millions of people who hold their shares in pension funds. It is already perverse that banks have to pay a higher rate of corporation tax than other businesses. One only has to look to the disastrous impact of windfall taxes on the North Sea to see what could follow any move to increase the surcharge further.

Business should know by now to take Labour’s warm words with a pinch of salt. In the run-up to the 2024 general election, the party wooed corporate Britain relentlessly. Rachel Reeves called Labour “the natural party of British business”. More than 120 business leaders signed an open letter backing the party, while the Confederation of British Industry welcomed Labour’s manifesto. Their reward has been two of the biggest tax-raising Budgets in history.

Mr Healey may need to find up to £35bn to meet existing spending commitments and boost defence, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. He must know that raising taxes to do so would have dire consequences for economic growth, which only seems to be limping along thanks to strong investment in artificial intelligence.

Too often, Labour politicians view the most successful parts of the economy as morally suspect. Mr Healey claims to understand that they are, in fact, national assets. The Budget is his chance to prove it.

data.title: Britain must maintain its lead to unlock energy’s holy grail
data.description:
It’s long been the “somewhere over the rainbow” promise of economic transformation that never seems to arrive. No, I’m not talking about AI, which, though already with us, has yet to prove the grandiose claims made of it.

Rather, I’m referring to nuclear fusion. This is the holy grail of energy production – the promise of limitless quantities of low-cost, carbon-free, baseload electricity.

Like the grail itself, commercialisation has thus far eluded even the world’s finest scientific minds and entrepreneurs.

But that doesn’t mean it’s still just science fiction. Lab-made fusion has already been successfully demonstrated on multiple occasions, and the science behind it is now relatively well advanced.

Yet until a few years ago, all such experimentation consumed more power than it generated, rendering it useless as an energy source.

As the old joke goes, economically viable fusion is about 30 years away, and will always be 30 years away. Harnessing the same power as the sun has proved much more difficult in practice than in theory.

In the past several years, however, there have been some very definite signs of the required breakthroughs.

And perhaps surprisingly, some of them are happening in Britain. With its history of academic excellence, the UK has always been good at this sort of stuff, but it has also been notably poor at commercialising it.

Innovative success has not translated well into economic exploitation. Rather, it is the US, and increasingly China, that tend to capitalise on what comes out of British brainpower.

Is fusion likely to suffer the same fate?

Dennis Whyte, who was this month appointed the chief executive of the UK Atomic Energy Authority – the Government body responsible for the nation’s “fusion strategy” – is determined that it should not. Formerly director of the fusion centre at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Whyte believes the UK has a unique set of capabilities that will allow it to excel in fusion’s development and commercialisation.

But first let’s talk about the potential, which to economic nerds like me is the really interesting bit.

Move over AI, the truly transformational technology coming down the road at us is not fully conscious humanoid robots but fusion.

Most economic progress is at root about energy and our ability to harness it to human purposes. At the heart of the industrial revolution, for instance, was not so much the machines themselves as the transformative power of coal.

The so-called Kardashev scale, though in some respects quack science, provides one way of charting economic advancement according to energy consumption.

Named after Nikolai Kardashev, the Soviet era astronomer, it seeks to measure progress in civilisation based entirely on the amount of energy that can be harnessed and deployed.

According to Kardashev, it’s only when humans manage to access unlimited quantities of it beyond mere Earth-bound sources that civilisation achieves its true potential.

This may or may not be an endorsement, but Elon Musk is particularly keen on the Kardashev way of thinking.

Only for him it’s about accessing the power of the sun via solar panels, battery storage and infrastructure in space. Indeed, he has dismissed pursuit of Earth-bound fusion reactors as “super dumb and farcical”.

Musk is the undisputed master of tech commercialisation, so he has to be taken seriously. Nonetheless, he should know better than anyone that progress involves, through a process of trial and error, testing the frontiers of science to virtual destruction and eventually finding a way through.

Think about it; if manmade fusion can be achieved at scale, it is likely to be a far bigger driver of productivity growth than anything AI can offer, as well as being a potential solution to any existential threat posed by climate change.

As Whyte points out, AI is a technology with unproven potential, despite the hundreds of billions of dollars being invested in it.

A lot of questions remain about its supposedly transformational powers, as last week’s wobble in AI-related stocks and shares seemed to confirm.

Nobody knows what its effect on jobs and growth might be, still less whether it is capable of generating the returns needed to justify the vast amounts being invested in it.

With energy, on the other hand, we already know what cheap power can do; fusion is moreover not just a further time-limited energy source, in the same way as a new gas field might be.

It is a forever, unlimited resource that promises to power hitherto undreamt levels of technological advancement and human progress. If it can be achieved, it truly would be a game changer, and as an economic leap forward, perhaps bigger than even the Industrial Revolution.

Interestingly, it is also complementary to the development of AI, which both has an insatiable appetite for power and whose computational skills are already helping to turbo-charge the pursuit of commercially viable fusion.

There is a developing symbiosis between the two, a mutually beneficial co-dependency which ought to help both technologies achieve their potential.

I’m no expert, so I cannot tell you if in 30 years’ time we’ll still be saying fusion is 30 years away and will always be 30 years away.

But Whyte knows as much as there is to know about fusion, and he’s never been more optimistic.

A growing number of labs and companies are successfully achieving it, including recently General Fusion Group, which has announced that its magnetised target fusion (MTF) technology has reached electron temperatures exceeding 12 million degrees Celsius, well in advance of what’s needed for fusion to take place.

The results were confirmed using the UK Atomic Energy Authority measurement techniques.

What’s more, around £10bn of private capital globally has been invested in fusion in a clear signal that commercialisation is beginning to be seen as eminently possible and even likely.

Not to be outdone, China is also chasing hard, having elevated fusion to a core strategic frontier and national infrastructure priority.

Some readers may be familiar with an Apple TV science fiction series called For All Mankind, which is based around the idea that the space race never ended.

The consequent superpower rivalry drives rapid technological progress, such that by the year 2000 space exploration and colonisation are far in advance of anything we see today.

The same rivalry already apparent between the West and China in AI is beginning to take hold in nuclear fusion, where China has a significant advantage in terms of the supply chains and manufacturing capacity needed to make fusion reactors a reality.

Still, Britain is for now very much part of the race. The UK was the first country in the world to produce nuclear power at scale for civilian use. It would be nice to think it is still capable of doing the same with fusion.

data.title: Airlines banned from charging parents to sit next to their children
data.description:
Airlines will be banned from charging parents extra to sit with their children on flights.

The Government has proposed a set of rules requiring airlines to seat children under the age of 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge.

According to the Department for Transport, it can cost a parent up to £104 to arrange to sit next to their child on a return journey.

Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking to correct a mistake.

It is thought ministers will bring in the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays.

MPs are debating a new set of rules for travel companies as the Civil Aviation (Consumer Protection and Regulatory Reform) Bill makes its way through Parliament.

The proposed law will give ministers powers to draw up a list of passenger rights and a list of duties which both airlines and airports must undertake.

‘Giving people room to breathe’

Andy Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

Rory Boland, the editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together.

“Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights.

The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children between two and 11 years old to pay to reserve what it referred to as a mandatory family seat. Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge.

The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority found.

At the time, Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair, said its previous policy was “the most progressive and transparent in Europe”.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the Government, airlines and trade unions working on a system to share information about disruptive passengers.

Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.

Using the information-sharing system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

“Everyone deserves to travel knowing their flight isn’t going to be disrupted by bad behaviour from a small minority,” Ms Alexander said.

“These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”

data.title: Putin has ordered ‘General Armageddon’ to smash the bridges of Kyiv. This is why
data.description:
As winter approaches, Vladimir Putin is resorting to the one weapon he has consistently used when his armies fail on the battlefield: terrorising civilians and smashing cities. He has just brought in General Sergei Surovikin – aka “General Armageddon” who flattened the Syrian city of Aleppo, killing thousands of civilians in the process – to do the same to Kyiv.

Putin needs something to change in Ukraine, as the Russian offensive in the Donbas has been in serious trouble for months. Ukrainian forces are pushing back around Pokrovsk and Lyman, while Russian casualties remain extraordinary. President Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed that more than 10,000 Russian soldiers were killed in a single week.

Whether that precise figure is ultimately verified or not, there is no doubt that Putin is paying a staggering price for very limited territorial gains. And now he is running short of men: it is getting difficult to recruit enough volunteer “kontraktniki” contract soldiers to replace the losses.

In theory, Putin could simply launch a mobilisation, which would yield huge numbers of new troops. But the Kremlin knows that another major mobilisation, potentially involving hundreds of thousands of Russians, could be politically explosive. The dictator therefore needs a dramatic change in the military equation before he is forced into a decision that could threaten his grip on power.

His answer is becoming increasingly obvious: if Russia cannot defeat Ukraine’s army, it will try to break the Ukrainian people and nation this winter. This is not a new tactic. Putin supported Bashar al-Assad’s brutal campaign in Syria, where I saw first hand what happened when hospitals, schools and civilian areas became targets for Russian firepower.

The calculation was simple: kill, wound and brutalise enough civilians – make their lives dangerous and horrible enough – and eventually they will demand that their own government ends the war. It failed in Syria. It is likely to fail in Ukraine too.

Kyiv is now under almost relentless attack. There were 18 air raid alerts in the capital on Tuesday alone. Russian missiles and drones are striking deep into the city, damaging civilian infrastructure and even hitting the National Academy of Sciences.

The seven bridges across the Dnipro are obvious targets. Kyiv, like most capital cities, is a major road and rail nexus. If it can be cut in half, that has a paralysing effect on the whole of northern Ukraine: imagine the effect on south eastern England if every bridge in London (including those on the M25) were down.

This is not the behaviour of a man preparing to end his war. It is the behaviour of a dictator preparing his population for a longer one.

The danger is that Putin has identified a vulnerability. Ukraine’s stocks of air-defence munitions are under enormous pressure. High-end interceptor missiles such as the US Patriot are in particularly short supply. Moscow knows this. It is therefore adapting its tactics, moving beyond military targets and increasingly seeking to cripple the infrastructure that allows Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities to function.

This is precisely why the West must understand what Putin is attempting before it is too late. His calculation has always been brutally simple: can Russia outlast its opponent? Putin believes it can.

He has shown an extraordinary willingness to sacrifice Russian soldiers. To the Kremlin, human life is a cheap commodity. Russia has a far larger population than Ukraine and has progressively placed its economy on a war footing. Putin therefore believes that Russia can absorb casualties for longer than Ukraine can stand the punishment and, crucially, for longer than Western governments can maintain public and political support.

That last is the real battle. The question is not simply whether Ukraine can hold Pokrovsk or Lyman. It is whether Britain and Europe have the political stamina to ensure that Ukraine is still standing next year, and the year after that.

I am not convinced that our Government fully understands this. The Prime Minister has explicitly stated that, to him, social security is more important than national security. His priorities are upside down. You cannot deliver social security if you are not secure as a nation.

The West must dramatically increase supplies of air-defence missiles, radars, drones and electronic-warfare systems. But we should also be prepared to consider measures that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago.

If Russia deliberately targets civilian infrastructure on an industrial scale, Nato must consider how its overwhelming air power could be used to protect Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure without directly entering the war. That does not necessarily mean declaring a traditional no-fly zone tomorrow. It means seriously examining whether Nato aircraft could help defend defined areas or critical infrastructure in extremis, particularly where the alternative is allowing Russian missiles and drones to slaughter civilians with impunity.

The Geneva Conventions are clear: the proper laws of war – not overblown human rights rules, but the regular laws of war – forbid deliberate targeting of civilians without any military purpose. Just when Ukraine appears to be gaining momentum on the battlefield, Putin is attempting to move the war on to ground where he believes Russia has the advantage: a test of civilian endurance.

We must not let him.

Ukraine’s army is fighting back in the Donbas. Its soldiers are inflicting enormous losses on the Russian military. This is precisely the moment when the West should be leaning forward, not stepping back. Putin understands strength, but understands weakness even better.

If we allow him to discover that bombing Kyiv works, he will do more of it. If, instead, Britain and Europe demonstrate that Ukraine’s cities will be defended, its people will be supported and its army will be supplied for as long as necessary, Putin may finally understand the one thing he has so far refused to accept: Russia cannot bomb and meat-grind its way to victory.

data.title: Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor under investigation
data.description:
Housing loans granted while Andy Burnham was Greater Manchester mayor are under investigation by councillors.

More than £1bn was lent to approximately 50 property developers – including three controlled by Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owner – by a fund managed by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) since 2015.

Councillors have now raised concerns about transparency and said the process to approve the loans was “out of kilter”.

John Leech, the chairman of the GMCA’s overview and scrutiny committee, told the BBC: “We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process.”

Mr Leech said the approval process had been criticised as “very opaque in the past and that it’s not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn’t”.

Earlier this month, The Telegraph revealed that the Prime Minister oversaw a £55m taxpayer loan to property companies ultimately controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan, the owner of Manchester City FC, while he was the mayor of Greater Manchester.

The decisions to issue the loans were taken in two meetings in 2017, both of which Mr Burnham chaired, evidencing that he was directly involved in decisions that favoured Abu Dhabi.

The loan scheme came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund, a pot of taxpayers’ money lent to the region by the central government based on the requirement that it would be used to tackle the housing crisis.

The fund was designed to provide loans for “projects which might otherwise struggle to secure financing”.

“In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn’t have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well,” Mr Leech, the Liberal Democrat opposition leader on Manchester city council, said. “And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015.”

Manchester Life is a joint venture set up in 2014 between Manchester city council and Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

ADUG was involved in three property developments with Manchester Life partially financed through the GMCA’s loan fund.

ADUG, Sheikh Mansour’s investment vehicle, has repaid the loans with interest, but the rate is not known.

A Manchester Life spokesman previously told The Telegraph that ADUG put its own capital into projects before accessing the loans, and that these loans were repayable external debt financing, commonly used by property developers.

The decisions to approve the loans were taken collectively by GMCA members, rather than by Mr Burnham alone.

The overview and scrutiny committee agreed to launch an inquiry into the loans earlier this year and, as newly elected chairman, Mr Leech is taking the investigation further.

He said the GMCA had been asked to produce a report about the use of the funds and the committee will question officers in a private meeting.

The committee does not have the power to sanction the mayor, but it can investigate, call witnesses, expose problems and challenge decisions.

Renaker, one of Manchester’s leading property developers, received the majority of the £1bn lent out from the fund.

Aubrey Weis, a rival developer, claims the loans were unfair subsidies, but in July, the Court of Appeal found there had been “no error of law” in the GMCA’s decision. Aubrey Weis is appealing the decision.

Mr Burnham has repeatedly praised the United Arab Emirates for investment that helped to transform the city, but it has not been clear until now that Sheikh Mansour’s contribution was partly financed by loans from taxpayers’ money.

Louie French, the shadow sports minister, said Mr Burnham had “serious questions to answer” about the loans.

“Taxpayers deserve transparency over how this money was awarded,” he said.

A GMCA spokesman said: “The Housing Investment Loan Fund was set up in 2015 with £300m of government funding to encourage, accelerate and unlock the building of new homes. Since then, this funding pot has been lent at commercial rates more than three times over, delivering 11,000 new homes and regenerating brownfield land across the city region, while providing new work for local people and Greater Manchester businesses.

“Decisions to grant loans from the fund are taken publicly. Not a single viable scheme was ever turned down and funds were lent to around 50 different developers.”

They added that the fund was open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector. 

The spokesman said: “Every penny loaned from the fund is being fully repaid, delivering billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer.

“Our share of the interest received on these loans, set to reach £37m by 2028, has gone back into work on our housing priorities, including building decent, affordable homes, launching the country’s first good landlord charter and training new housing enforcement officers to drive up standards for renters.

“We are supporting the scrutiny and oversight committee with their enquiries.”

data.title: Netflix must return to quality TV to halt its decline
data.description:
If you added plenty of scenes of stressed-looking suits slamming doors and running down corridors, the current saga at Netflix would make a pretty good corporate drama. The streaming giant last week dramatically replaced its chief content officer, at the same time as announcing a deep round of layoffs.

It is not hard to understand what Ted Sarandos, Netflix’s co-chief executive in charge of content, is doing. With viewing numbers stagnating, and the share price sliding on Wall Street, the streaming platform is at risk of losing its dominant position in the industry, having once looked unassailable. Only a return to high-quality, innovative programming is going to save Netflix’s position at the top now – and that is going to prove to be very expensive.

It’s a far cry from what is on offer these days. A Jennifer Aniston movie, a documentary about an ageing pop/football/movie star, followed by a sequel to the Jennifer Aniston movie, except this time with a cute puppy. Anyone flicking through the Netflix home screen during the last year may well have noticed that its schedule might be described as, to put it politely, tired. Now even the company itself appears to have realised.

Even so, it no longer has the impregnable lock on the industry that it once had.

Now there are a whole range of choices, and with the acquisition of Warner Brothers by Paramount, the market will become even more brutally competitive. Netflix has turned into just one choice among many.

Competition is just part of the problem. Its real problem is this: management has been pursuing a very short-sighted strategy. Netflix has dramatically pushed up its prices, while adding advertising to the mix, with extra charges to avoid them. Here in the UK for example, the monthly cost has risen from £4.99 for the standard tier, including ads, to £7.99, while the premium monthly subscription has risen from £13.99 to £20.99. It is much the same story in the rest of the world. The monthly cost has gone up by more than the rate of inflation.

At the same time, the quality of the programming has gone down. Of course, to some degree that is a subjective judgment, and not everyone likes the same TV shows. But Netflix has been winning fewer major awards over the last few years, and HBO has now finished before it for Emmy nominations for the last two years running. It still has the occasional prestige film or drama, such as Guillermo del Toro’s version of Frankenstein and the newly released East of Eden. But they are starting to become very few and far between.

Netflix is still spending $20bn (£15bn) a year on content, but the spending has not been going up at the same rate as prices. By contrast, Disney is spending $24bn (all those Star Wars spin-offs don’t come cheap) with fewer subscribers. Netflix first broke through with high-quality prestige drama such as House of Cards and The Crown. It created event television that everyone talked about, and made a compelling case for keeping the monthly subscription. Over the last few years, it has concentrated more on pushing up prices, while churning out cheaper, often formulaic dramas.

True, that is great for the bottom line, and it keeps profits buoyant. Yet subscribers are being asked to pay more and more for less and less. Sooner or later they are going to notice.

There is only one real fix. The way to keep its dominant position in the market is to moderate price rises and return to high-quality drama. It would be easy for Netflix to rest on its laurels, keep squeezing its subscribers with higher charges to make as much money as possible. But it is not going to work.

Netflix needs to level with its shareholders, explain to them that profits are going to be lower for a few years but that this is necessary as it has to invest more in programmes to fend off the competition. It will be expensive. But nothing else will work. So long as Wall Street is thinking straight, investors will back this strategy.
